The **Atacama Desert** is a desert plateau in **South America**, mostly in **northern Chile** and in some places stretching toward southern **Peru**. It is widely considered the **driest non-polar desert in the world**, and some weather stations in its interior have gone many years without recording any significant rainfall. The desert sits between the **Pacific Ocean** on the west and the **Andes Mountains** on the east, forming a narrow strip that runs north to south along the Pacific coast.

The Atacama covers about **105,000 square kilometres** (around 41,000 sq mi), although some broader definitions include nearby arid lands as well. Its extreme dryness comes from a combination of factors: the **cold Humboldt Current** offshore reduces evaporation and cloud formation, the **subtropical high-pressure system** limits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air coming from the Amazon Basin. Because of this, much of the region gets only a few millimetres of rain each year, and some central areas can go decades without measurable precipitation.

Even with such harsh conditions, the Atacama supports specialized life. Plant life is sparse in the hyper-arid core, but cacti, shrubs, and tough grasses grow in less extreme areas. Coastal fog, known locally as **camanchaca**, supplies moisture that helps sustain some ecosystems. The desert is also home to insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to dry conditions, while high-altitude wetlands and salt flats provide habitat for flamingos and other Andean species.

People have lived in the desert for a very long time, including Indigenous groups such as the **Atacameño**, or **Likan Antai**, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. European colonization brought the region under Spanish control, and in the 19th century the Atacama became economically important because of its rich deposits of **nitrates**, **copper**, and other minerals. Disputes over these resources helped lead to the **War of the Pacific** (1879–1884), after which Chile took control of large desert territories that had previously belonged to Peru and Bolivia.

Today, the Atacama is still a major centre of **mining**, especially for copper and **lithium**. It is also internationally known for **astronomy**. With its high elevation, very little cloud cover, low humidity, and low light pollution, it is one of the best places on Earth for observing the night sky. Major observatories in or near the region include the **Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)** and several facilities on **Cerro Paranal** and **La Silla**.

The Atacama is also an important destination for **tourism** and scientific research. Its striking landscapes feature salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Because its dry conditions resemble those on Mars, the desert has been used as an analogue environment for testing space exploration technology and for studying the limits of life in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city can feel, at first, like stepping into a life meant for someone braver than you. The decision usually starts out as an idea: a job offer, a school, a relationship, or just a vague desire to reinvent yourself. On paper, the move seems neat and intentional. In real life, it looks more like cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, GPS directions in a robotic voice, and the quiet jolt of waking up in a room where the light hits the wall differently. The good parts and the hard parts of moving show up at the same time, so tightly tangled that it can be difficult to tell them apart.

One of the best things about a new city is the chance to see yourself differently. In the place where you have always lived, your identity can start to feel fixed through repetition. You are someone’s child, someone’s friend, the person who orders the usual at the coffee shop or avoids certain streets because of old memories. In a new city, no one knows your history unless you decide to share it. That kind of anonymity can feel lonely, but it can also be freeing. You can be more social, or more private. You can experiment with new routines, new neighborhoods, even new versions of your personality. The city does not care who you used to be; it only asks how you are going to live in it now.

There is also the plain, vivid pleasure of discovery. A new city can make everyday life feel a little like exploration. Even buying groceries becomes a small expedition. You notice the architecture, the slang, the weather, the way people stand in line or greet strangers. You figure out where to get the best bread, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform crowds up fastest when it rains. These details build slowly, and each one makes the unfamiliar place feel less like a map and more like a home. Moving reminds you that daily life is not as fixed as it can seem; it can still surprise you.

But the costs are real, and they are often harder to measure than rent or moving trucks. The clearest one is homesickness, though that word can sound too gentle for what it sometimes feels like. Homesickness is not just about missing people. It is about missing the version of yourself that fit naturally around them. In your old city, you knew how to belong without thinking about it. In the new one, belonging takes effort. You have to build a life almost from the ground up: find a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, and a person to call when something breaks. Even small errands can wear you out when you have to do them without the comfort of familiarity.

Then there is the emotional math of distance. Moving often means accepting that love will be less convenient. Friendships that once depended on proximity now have to survive on texts, scheduled calls, and expensive visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back home only to realize that “home” has kept changing while you were away. The city you left does not sit still, faithfully waiting for your return. It keeps moving, just as you do. There is real grief in understanding that.

And maybe that is part of what makes moving worthwhile: it teaches you that a life can grow only by being unsettled. A new city offers freedom, novelty, and growth, but the price is uncertainty, loneliness, and loss. Moving means agreeing to that trade. With time, if you are lucky, the strange streets start to feel like your streets. The costs do not go away, but they begin to feel less like punishments and more like the price of becoming larger than the life you used to know.

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday that it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients, adding to growing concerns about cybersecurity weaknesses in the healthcare industry.

The network, which runs several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region, said it detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. In a statement, officials said the organization acted quickly to contain the incident, started an internal investigation, and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to figure out how far the breach may have reached.

Early findings indicate that unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records containing names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, insurance information, and, in some cases, limited clinical details. Hospital officials said there is no current evidence that financial account or payment card information was compromised, although the investigation is still underway.

“We take the privacy and security of our patients’ information extremely seriously,” the hospital network said in its statement. “Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected.”

The hospital network did not say exactly how many patients were involved, but it described the breach as “significant.” People affected are expected to be notified by mail in the coming weeks. As a precaution, the organization said it will provide complimentary credit monitoring and identity protection services to eligible patients.

Hospital operations have continued during the investigation, although some administrative systems were temporarily taken offline, leading to delays in scheduling and access to certain online services. According to officials, emergency departments and inpatient care were not affected.

Cybersecurity experts say healthcare organizations continue to be appealing targets for hackers because of the amount of sensitive personal and medical data they store. Unlike stolen credit card numbers, medical records can include permanent identifying information that may be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing schemes.

“This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients,” said one data privacy analyst who is not affiliated with the hospital network. “Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved.”

Regulators are expected to review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, which requires covered entities to protect patient information and notify individuals when certain breaches happen.

Patients are being urged to stay alert for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls related to their medical care. The hospital network said it is strengthening its system security, reviewing access controls, and taking additional measures to help prevent similar incidents in the future.

A good teacher isn’t just someone who knows a subject well. Knowledge matters, of course, but information by itself doesn’t inspire curiosity, build confidence, or change a student’s life. In my view, what makes a good teacher is a mix of patience, passion, empathy, and the ability to make students feel seen. The best teachers do more than teach lessons; they create an environment where learning feels possible.

One of the most important qualities a teacher can have is patience. Not every student learns at the same speed, and not every person thinks in the same way. A good teacher understands that. Instead of getting frustrated when a student struggles, they try a different explanation, a new example, or another approach. Patience sends a powerful message: difficulty is not the same as failure, and understanding sometimes takes time. For students who doubt themselves, that can make all the difference. A patient teacher teaches more than a subject—they teach perseverance.

Passion is another essential quality. Students can tell when a teacher genuinely cares about what they are teaching. Enthusiasm is contagious. A teacher who talks about literature, science, history, or mathematics with real interest can make even a hard topic feel alive. Passion brings energy into the classroom. It turns lessons from a list of facts into something meaningful and memorable. More than that, it shows students that learning is not just an obligation, but something that can bring joy.

Empathy matters just as much. A good teacher remembers what it feels like to be confused, nervous, or afraid of making mistakes. They know that students often carry invisible burdens: family problems, stress, insecurity, loneliness, or pressure to succeed. Because of that, they treat students with kindness and respect. They listen. They notice when someone is quieter than usual or seems discouraged. Sometimes the most important thing a teacher can offer is not an explanation, but encouragement at the right moment. A student who feels understood is more likely to participate, take risks, and believe in their ability to improve.

Good teachers also know how to challenge their students. Being kind does not mean lowering standards. In fact, some of the most effective teachers expect a great deal because they see their students’ potential. They push students to think more deeply, work more carefully, and aim higher than they might on their own. What makes this work is that those high expectations are matched with support. They do not just demand excellence; they help students achieve it.

Finally, a good teacher leaves a lasting impact that reaches beyond the classroom. Years later, students may forget certain lessons, dates, or formulas, but they often remember how a teacher made them feel. They remember the teacher who believed in them when they doubted themselves, who sparked an interest they had never thought about before, or who showed them that their voice mattered. In that way, teaching is not only about education, but also about shaping character and possibility.

To me, a good teacher is someone who combines knowledge with humanity. They guide, challenge, encourage, and inspire. They help students learn not only about the world, but also about themselves. That is why the influence of a truly good teacher can last a lifetime.

# Commit Message Style Guide

Good commit messages make it easier for teammates to review changes, help future maintainers understand why decisions were made, and make `git log` and `git blame` much more useful when you’re debugging. Use these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```text
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Put a blank line between the subject and the body. For trivial changes, the body and footer are optional.

## Subject Line

- **Keep it to 50 characters.** The absolute maximum is 72.
- **Write in the imperative mood**: “Add retry logic,” not “Added retry logic” or “Adds retry logic.” A good check is whether it completes the sentence, “If applied, this commit will…”
- **Capitalize the first word.**
- **Do not end with a period.**
- **Be specific.** “Fix bug” and “Update code” don’t tell the reader anything. “Fix null check in user lookup” does.

If your team uses prefixes like `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:` as part of Conventional Commits, use them consistently and make sure the full subject still stays within the limit.

## Body

Use the body to explain **what changed and why**, not how. The diff already shows how it was done. It can help to cover things like:

- What problem led to this change?
- Why was this approach chosen instead of another?
- Are there side effects or limitations reviewers should know about?

Wrap lines at 72 characters. For lists of separate changes, use bullets with hyphens or asterisks.

## Footer

Use the footer for metadata, such as:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope of a Commit

Each commit should represent one logical change. If your subject needs an “and,” that may be a sign the commit should be split. Avoid combining formatting changes with functional changes, because that makes both review and reverts more difficult.

## Examples

**Weak:**
```text
fixed stuff
```

**Strong:**
```text
Fix race condition in session cleanup

The cleanup job could delete sessions that were being
refreshed concurrently, logging users out unexpectedly.
Acquire a row-level lock before checking expiration.

Fixes #482
```

## Things to Avoid

- Vague messages like “WIP,” “misc fixes,” or “updates”
- Describing the file instead of the change
- Referring only to context you have, like “as discussed”
- Blaming or editorializing, like “fix stupid bug”
- Committing generated noise without explaining it

## Final Check

Before you commit, ask yourself: *Would someone reading this in two years understand why this change was made?* If the answer is no, add more context.

# Tbilisi

**Tbilisi** (Georgian: თბილისი), historically called **Tiflis**, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It sits on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River and had a population of about 1.2 million in the early 2020s, which is roughly a third of the country’s population. It is one of the South Caucasus’s main cultural, economic, and transportation centers.

## History

According to tradition, the city was founded in the 5th century AD by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia, who is said to have discovered the area’s warm sulfur springs while hunting. The name comes from the Old Georgian word *tbili*, meaning “warm.” His successors later moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city became increasingly important despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and various Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi reached a high point during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries. It was later sacked several times, including by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. In the early 19th century, Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a short period of independence from 1918 to 1921, the city became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991, and since then Tbilisi has gone through political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, along with major modernization.

## Geography and climate

Tbilisi lies in a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at an elevation of about 400 to 770 meters above sea level. Its climate is transitional between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

Tbilisi is especially known for its mix of architectural styles, combining medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary influences. The Old Town, or Dzveli Tbilisi, is marked by narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Major landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sioni Cathedral, Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda, or “Mother of Georgia,” statue stands above the city on Sololaki Ridge.

The city is home to many theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian cuisine is a big part of local identity, with dishes such as *khachapuri* and *khinkali*, along with local wines. Tbilisi’s nightlife and electronic music scene have also attracted international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is Georgia’s financial and commercial center. Its major sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, which opened in 1966, is the city’s main rapid transit system, and it is supported by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the country’s main gateway.

## See also

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

The Old Town, or Dzveli Tbilisi, is marked by narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Major landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sioni Cathedral, Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda, or “Mother of Georgia,” statue stands above the city on Sololaki Ridge.

The city is home to many theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian cuisine is a big part of local identity, with dishes such as *khachapuri* and *khinkali*, along with local wines. Tbilisi’s nightlife and electronic music scene have also attracted international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is Georgia’s financial and commercial center. Its major sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, which opened in 1966, is the city’s main rapid transit system, and it is supported by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the country’s main gateway.

Maplewood County saw an unusually large turnout Tuesday for its school board election, with residents voting in numbers not seen in decades. Election officials said 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots to choose three school board members — more than twice the turnout of the last school board election and the highest participation ever recorded for a stand-alone local race in the county.

According to the County Elections Office, 38,214 of the district’s 93,200 registered voters took part, compared with about 17 percent two years ago. At several precincts, lines stretched out the door during the after-work rush. At Lincoln Elementary, polls stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so everyone already in line could vote.

“We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this,” said Dolores Whitfield, the county’s elections director. “By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle.”

People watching the race pointed to a heated campaign centered on a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, and disputes over curriculum and class sizes. Six candidates ran for the three open seats, and the contest brought unusually heavy campaign spending for a local race, along with a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation issue organized door-knocking campaigns and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School also held a voter registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

“I’ve lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year,” said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. “Decisions about my kids’ classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say.”

Others said the stakes were simply too high to sit out. “Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there,” said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman in the lead, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who currently hold the other two winning spots. Fewer than 400 votes separate third and fourth place, and the elections office said results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office plans to review how the day was handled so it can be better prepared for future high-turnout elections. “This is a good problem to have,” she said. “We hope it’s a sign of lasting engagement.”

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe operated by NASA that launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program. It was built mainly to study the outer Solar System, but it went on to become one of the most important scientific spacecraft ever flown. After finishing its original mission, it kept traveling outward and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The spacecraft was built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard a Titan IIIE rocket. Even though it lifted off after its twin, Voyager 2, it took a faster path that let it reach Jupiter and Saturn first. Its journey made use of a rare planetary alignment that allowed spacecraft to visit multiple outer planets with the help of gravitational assists.

Voyager 1 had its first major encounter with Jupiter in 1979. During that flyby, it sent back detailed images of the planet’s atmosphere, including its chaotic cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. It also made major discoveries about Jupiter’s moons, most famously finding evidence of active volcanism on Io, the first volcanic activity ever observed beyond Earth. In addition, it gathered new information about Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, along with Jupiter’s magnetosphere and ring system.

In 1980, Voyager 1 passed Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a major target because of its thick atmosphere. The probe confirmed that Titan’s atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, although its dense haze kept scientists from seeing the surface in detail. Voyager 1 also returned extensive data on Saturn’s rings, moons, and magnetic environment. Because the Titan flyby required a specific trajectory, the spacecraft was sent out of the plane of the Solar System, which ended any chance of visiting more planets.

Once its planetary mission was over, Voyager 1 moved into an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region shaped by the solar wind. In August 2012, NASA announced that Voyager 1 had become the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space by crossing the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Since then, its instruments have continued measuring charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma conditions in this still poorly understood region.

Voyager 1 also carries the Golden Record, a phonograph record filled with sounds, images, and messages meant to represent the diversity of life and culture on Earth. It was conceived as a symbolic message for any future finders and has become one of the mission’s most lasting cultural legacies.

As of the 21st century, Voyager 1 is still in contact with Earth through NASA’s Deep Space Network, although its power supply slowly declines as its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produce less output. The mission has been extended many times, and the spacecraft continues to send back valuable scientific data as it travels farther into interstellar space.

## Pivot Tables User Guide

A pivot table is a quick way to summarize and analyze large amounts of spreadsheet data. Instead of manually sorting, filtering, or building formulas, you can use one to group information, calculate totals, and spot trends more easily.

### When to Use a Pivot Table
A pivot table is useful when you need to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records, such as customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange data without changing the original table
- Explore patterns in large datasets

### Before You Begin
For the best results, make sure your source data:
- Is arranged in rows and columns
- Has a single header row
- Does not contain completely blank rows or columns
- Uses consistent data types within each column, such as dates, numbers, or text

Your source data might include columns like `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a Pivot Table
1. Click any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where you want the pivot table to go:
   - New worksheet
   - Existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

You’ll then see a blank pivot table layout along with a field list.

### Understanding the Pivot Table Areas
Most pivot table tools have four main layout areas:

- **Rows**: Shows categories vertically
- **Columns**: Shows categories horizontally
- **Values**: Displays calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: Lets you limit the data that appears

### Building a Basic Pivot Table
If you want to summarize total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** into **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** into **Values**.

The pivot table will display each region and its total revenue.

If you want to compare revenue by region and product:
1. Leave **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** into **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing Calculations
A value field can usually be summarized in different ways, including:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change the calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or in the field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Select the calculation you want.

### Filtering and Sorting
You can refine your results by:
- Applying a report filter, such as showing only one year
- Sorting row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expanding or collapsing grouped items

### Refreshing the Pivot Table
If your source data changes, refresh the pivot table so the results update:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Choose **Refresh** from the pivot table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Use clear column names in your source data
- Format numbers so they are easier to read, such as currency or percentages
- If dates are not grouping correctly, make sure they are stored as real dates
- Leave the source data unchanged and use the pivot table for analysis

Pivot tables are powerful because they let you reorganize data instantly, which makes reporting and decision-making faster and easier.

# Pivot Tables: A User Guide

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table is a quick way to summarize large datasets without using formulas. It helps you group, count, total, and average your data, and you can rearrange it in seconds to look at it from different angles. It’s useful when you need answers to questions like “What were total sales by region?” or “How many orders did each rep close per month?”

## Before You Begin

Before creating a pivot table, make sure your data is set up properly:

- **Include headers.** Every column should have a unique, nonblank title.
- **Avoid blank rows or columns.** These can cause the pivot table to miss data.
- **Keep data consistent.** Each column should contain only one type of information, such as dates only or numbers only.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell within your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and select **Pivot Table**.
3. Check that the displayed data range is correct.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table: a new sheet is recommended, but you can also use an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

You’ll see an empty pivot table appear, along with a field panel that lists your column headers.

## Understanding the Four Areas

The field panel has four boxes. You build your report by dragging fields into these areas:

- **Rows:** Categories that appear down the left side, such as Product.
- **Columns:** Categories that appear across the top, such as Quarter.
- **Values:** The numbers being calculated, such as Sum of Revenue.
- **Filters:** Fields that let you limit the entire table to specific items, such as a single year.

## Example

Let’s say your data includes the columns Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. If you want to see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** into Rows.
2. Drag **Month** into Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** into Values.

The pivot table will show total revenue for each region-month combination, with grand totals around the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

Numeric fields are summed by default. If you want a different calculation, click the field in the Values box, choose **Value Field Settings**, and select another option, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also show values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- **Sort:** Click the dropdown arrow next to a row or column label.
- **Filter:** Use that same arrow to uncheck items you want to hide.
- **Group:** Right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- **Rearrange:** Drag fields from one area to another to view the data in different ways.

## Keeping Data Current

Pivot tables do not update automatically when the source data changes. To update one, right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you’ve added new rows, you may also need to update the source range using **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- **Numbers are counted instead of summed:** The column probably contains text or blanks. Clean up the data and refresh the pivot table.
- **Dates won’t group:** Some date entries may be stored as text instead of actual dates. Convert them to true dates.

With a little practice, pivot tables can become one of the fastest ways to analyze data.

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she’d grown up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were cloudy, and the brass had long been stripped from the ticket counter. But she put her palm flat against the waiting room wall as if she were checking whether a sleeping animal was still breathing. “I left for the city from this bench,” she said. “Your grandfather proposed on that platform.” By any architect’s standards, it wasn’t a remarkable building. But to her, it was the hinge her whole life had turned on.

I think about that moment whenever I hear someone say old buildings are just obstacles—too expensive to maintain, too inconvenient to retrofit, taking up space where something newer and shinier could be built. It’s not a stupid argument. Old buildings leak. They fight every attempt at new wiring. They often don’t meet modern codes, and nostalgia doesn’t pay for a new roof. I don’t think every old structure should be saved. A building isn’t automatically sacred just because it managed to survive.

But some are worth saving, and I’ve come to believe the reasons are practical as much as emotional.

For one thing, old buildings hold a kind of memory that no archive can really reproduce. A photograph can show you what a street looked like. A building lets you step inside the scale of another time. You notice how low the ceilings were, how narrow the stairs, how much daylight mattered when rooms depended on windows instead of switches. History stops feeling abstract when you have to duck to get through its doorway.

They also preserve a level of craftsmanship we mostly no longer pay for. In the library in my hometown—a century-old building where I spent a lot of time as a teenager—someone had carved tiny acorns into the banister. No one had to do that. No budget meeting today would sign off on it. And yet generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns, and I think it taught us something without ever saying it out loud: ordinary places could still be made with care.

Then there’s the quieter case for continuity. Neighborhoods built entirely from new construction can feel strangely weightless, like stage sets waiting for a story to happen. Old buildings give a place the feeling that people have actually lived there. They give newcomers and lifelong residents a landmark in common, even if what they remember about it isn’t the same. That shared point of reference becomes part of the social fabric, and fabric is a lot easier to tear than it is to weave.

And finally, there’s the simple issue of waste. Preservationists like to say the greenest building is often the one that’s already standing. Tearing one down throws away all the energy and materials already built into it, and it fills landfills too.

The train station was eventually demolished and replaced with a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn’t. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were sharp, and there was nothing there to suggest that a departure—or a proposal—had ever taken place on that spot.

That’s what I wish skeptics understood. We don’t preserve buildings because stone and timber are inherently precious. We preserve them because they keep the places where our lives took shape. And once they’re gone, the bench is gone too, and the palm against the wall, and the proof.

The **Battle of Hastings** took place on **14 October 1066** between the army of **William, Duke of Normandy**, and the forces of **King Harold Godwinson** of England. It was the decisive battle of the **Norman Conquest of England** and led to the start of Norman rule. Although it is traditionally named after the nearby town of Hastings, the fighting actually happened about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, near what is now the town of **Battle** in East Sussex.

The battle grew out of a dispute over who should inherit the English throne. After **Edward the Confessor** died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William of Normandy, though, argued that Edward had previously promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to back his claim. There was also a third rival, **Harald Hardrada** of Norway, who invaded England as well. Harold Godwinson defeated and killed Hardrada at the **Battle of Stamford Bridge** on 25 September 1066, but the win left his army worn out.

At the same time, William crossed the English Channel and landed at **Pevensey** on 28 September 1066. He then moved into Sussex, where he built a prefabricated castle at Hastings and raided the surrounding countryside, in part to lure Harold south. Harold marched quickly from London with his household troops, the **housecarls**, along with the shire levies known as the **fyrd**.

The two sides met on **Senlac Hill**. Harold’s men formed a tight **shield wall** along the ridge, while William’s army was made up of **infantry, archers, and cavalry**, in keeping with Norman military practice. The battle lasted for most of the day and was fiercely contested. Early Norman attacks were driven back by the English line. At one point, rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have raised his helmet to show he was still alive and to rally his men.

A key turning point came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while chasing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were real or staged, but they gave Norman cavalry the chance to isolate and destroy sections of Harold’s army. Late in the day, Harold himself was killed, traditionally said to have been hit in the eye by an arrow, though the exact way he died remains uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility killed, resistance collapsed.

William’s victory cleared the way for his coronation as **King William I of England** on **25 December 1066**. The battle reshaped English society, aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. The **Battle of Hastings** took place on **14 October 1066** between the army of **William, Duke of Normandy**, and the forces of **King Harold Godwinson** of England. It was the decisive battle of the **Norman Conquest of England** and led to the start of Norman rule. Although it is traditionally named after the nearby town of Hastings, the fighting actually happened about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, near what is now the town of **Battle** in East Sussex.

The battle grew out of a dispute over who should inherit the English throne. After **Edward the Confessor** died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William of Normandy, though, argued that Edward had previously promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to back his claim. There was also a third rival, **Harald Hardrada** of Norway, who invaded England as well. Harold Godwinson defeated and killed Hardrada at the **Battle of Stamford Bridge** on 25 September 1066, but the win left his army worn out.

At the same time, William crossed the English Channel and landed at **Pevensey** on 28 September 1066. He then moved into Sussex, where he built a prefabricated castle at Hastings and raided the surrounding countryside, in part to lure Harold south. Harold marched quickly from London with his household troops, the **housecarls**, along with the shire levies known as the **fyrd**.

The two sides met on **Senlac Hill**. Harold’s men formed a tight **shield wall** along the ridge, while William’s army was made up of **infantry, archers, and cavalry**, in keeping with Norman military practice. The battle lasted for most of the day and was fiercely contested. Early Norman attacks were driven back by the English line. At one point, rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have raised his helmet to show he was still alive and to rally his men.

A key turning point came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while chasing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were real or staged, but they gave Norman cavalry the chance to isolate and destroy sections of Harold’s army. Late in the day, Harold himself was killed, traditionally said to have been hit in the eye by an arrow, though the exact way he died remains uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility killed, resistance collapsed.

William’s victory cleared the way for his coronation as **King William I of England** on **25 December 1066**. The battle reshaped English society, aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. It has been commemorated in sources such as the **Bayeux Tapestry**, one of the most important visual records of the conquest.

# Transit Strike Shuts Down Buses and Trains, Stranding Thousands of Commuters

**Union turns down final offer after overnight talks fall apart; city prepares for a second day of disruption**

Hundreds of thousands of commuters were left scrambling for other ways to get around Monday after public-transit workers went on strike at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the metro area.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents about 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station workers, started the strike at 4 a.m. after contract talks with the Regional Transit Authority collapsed late Sunday. It is the first systemwide strike in 14 years.

“We didn’t want it to come to this,” union president Dolores Reyes said from a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. “But the people who keep this city moving can’t be expected to fall behind on rent while costs keep going up every year.”

The union is asking for a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials offered a 5 percent raise and said they could not agree to the other demands without either raising fares or cutting routes.

“Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible,” Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. “We’re still at the table and urge the union to come back to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives.”

The effects were felt right away. Highways were already jammed before sunrise, and traffic officials said delays were running as much as 70 percent longer than usual. Ride-share fares jumped, and bike-share stations downtown were cleared out by 8 a.m. Several large employers told staff to work from home if they could.

At Central Station, which is usually crowded with morning commuters, only a few people stood reading closure notices. Marcus Hill, who works in a hospital cafeteria, said he had already walked two miles before a friend was able to drive him the rest of the way.

“I support the drivers, I really do,” Hill said. “But I can’t afford to miss shifts either. I’m stuck in the middle.”

Schools reported more absences than usual, and the district said yellow school buses would continue running because they are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is still running at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, although advocates say wait times have stretched past two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho urged both sides to get back into talks immediately and said the city would provide staff to help mediate. “Every day this goes on hurts working families and local businesses,” she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million a day in lost productivity and sales.

No new bargaining session has been scheduled. The union said it will keep picketing until it gets what it called a “serious proposal,” while the Authority said it is making contingency plans in case the stoppage drags on.

Some old buildings are worth preserving not just because they’ve been around a long time, but because they still mean something. Being old by itself isn’t enough. A cracked wall or a faded sign doesn’t become important simply because it managed to survive. But some buildings hold something bigger than themselves: memory, craftsmanship, identity, and the quiet traces of how people once imagined their lives. Preserving them isn’t really about freezing the past. It’s about keeping a conversation alive between generations.

I think of old buildings as a kind of public memory. Families hold on to photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can carry feeling in a way that facts alone can’t. Cities and towns need that too. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, church, or row of apartments can reveal more about the people who built a place than any plaque ever could. The width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the wear in the stone steps—details like these remind us that history was lived in a physical way. Someone walked up those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news, for work, for love, or for grief to ease. When buildings like that are lost, part of our shared memory goes with them.

Old buildings also deserve to be preserved because they offer a kind of beauty that’s difficult to recreate. Many were built with patience, strong materials, and a level of ornament or care that reflected pride more than efficiency. Even simple buildings often show a human touch: uneven bricks laid by hand, wooden floors polished by decades of footsteps, windows placed not only for function but for grace. At a time when so much construction is shaped by speed and profit, these older buildings remind us that beauty and usefulness don’t have to be in conflict. They teach us to value texture, permanence, and detail.

There’s an ethical reason to preserve them too. Demolishing and rebuilding isn’t always the same thing as progress. Sometimes it’s amnesia dressed up as development. Of course, not every old building can or should be saved. Cities need to evolve, and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, preserving it becomes a way of showing respect. It says that the people who came before us are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still matter. That’s especially true for places connected to ordinary people, not only the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion ever could.

What moves me most is the way preserved buildings make time feel layered rather than lost. Walking into an old library or courthouse can make you feel, even for a moment, that your own life belongs to a much longer human story. The building has survived fashions, governments, and private worries. It has witnessed generations and is still standing, asking for care instead of pity. At its best, preservation is an act of humility. It recognizes that we are not the first people to love a place, and we won’t be the last to need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the Docs

Thanks for helping us improve the documentation. Whether you’re fixing a typo or writing a brand-new tutorial, every contribution makes the project easier to use. This guide will help you get started.

## Ways to contribute

There are lots of ways to help:

- **Fix errors:** typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples.
- **Improve clarity:** rewrite confusing sections or add missing context.
- **Write new content:** tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages.
- **Review pull requests:** a fresh set of eyes can make a big difference.
- **Report issues:** if you notice a problem but can’t fix it yourself, open an issue.

## Getting set up

1. **Fork** the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000` to watch your changes update live.

If you’re making a small edit, you can also click **Edit this page** at the bottom of any page to make changes directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, like `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. The files are written in Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting, and `npm run build` to make sure the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit your changes with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Consistent writing makes the docs easier to read. Please follow these conventions:

- **Use plain language.** Keep sentences short and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- **Address the reader as "you."**
- **Use active voice.** Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- **Put code in code blocks** and include the language for syntax highlighting.
- **Use sentence case** for headings.
- **Make examples runnable.** Test every snippet before you submit it.
- **Write descriptive link text.** Avoid phrases like "click here."

## Structure of the docs

We organize the documentation into four content types:

- **Tutorials:** step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- **How-to guides:** solutions to specific problems.
- **Reference:** precise technical descriptions.
- **Explanations:** background information and concepts.

Try to keep each page focused on just one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before you submit, make sure that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will usually respond within a few days. We may suggest edits, so please don’t be discouraged by feedback. That’s a normal part of working together. Once your pull request is approved, your changes will be merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Please be kind, patient, and respectful. All contributors are expected to follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

If you have questions, ask in our discussion forum or leave a comment on an issue. We’re always happy to help first-time contributors get started.

The Hanseatic League was a commercial and defensive alliance of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. From the late 12th century to the 17th century, it dominated maritime trade in the Baltic and North Seas. At its height, it connected nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen, and played a major role in the economic, political, and urban development of medieval northern Europe.

The League grew out of the expansion of German merchants, especially from cities like Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and special trading privileges abroad. Lübeck, founded in 1143 and strategically positioned between the North and Baltic Seas, became the League’s leading city. By the 13th century, merchant communities from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts, known as *Kontore*, in major foreign centers such as London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These settlements functioned as warehouses, offices, and legal communities that helped safeguard Hanseatic interests.

The Hanseatic League was not a state, and it had no formal constitution, permanent army, or centralized administration. Instead, it operated as a loose association of towns and merchants bound together by shared economic interests. Decisions were made at assemblies called the *Hansetag*, where representatives from member cities worked out commercial policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership was flexible, and cities participated to varying degrees.

The League’s economic strength came from the exchange of regional goods. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish came from the east, while cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built efficient shipping networks and adopted standardized commercial practices that reduced transaction costs and increased trust over long distances. When necessary, the League also used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, as it did in conflicts with Denmark during the 14th century.

Beginning in the late 15th century, the Hanseatic League went into a gradual decline. The rise of stronger territorial states, the shift of trade routes toward the Atlantic, increasing Dutch and English competition, and internal divisions all weakened its influence. Its overseas trading privileges were steadily reduced, and several *Kontore* were closed. Although some cities continued to identify with the League, its political importance had largely disappeared by the 17th century. The last meeting of the *Hansetag* was held in 1669.

The Hanseatic League left a lasting mark on the urban culture, architecture, and commercial law of northern Europe. Many former Hanseatic cities, including Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn, still preserve distinctive brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions tied to the League. In modern historiography, it is often seen as an early example of transnational commercial cooperation and urban networking in European history.

# Bike-Share FAQ

## Getting Started

**How do I rent a bike?**  
Start by downloading our app and creating an account. Once you're set up, find a nearby station, tap “Unlock,” and scan the bike’s QR code. If you prefer, you can also unlock bikes at station kiosks with a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**  
Here’s the pricing:

- **Single ride:** $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute  
- **Day pass:** $12 for unlimited 30-minute rides over 24 hours  
- **Monthly membership:** $20 for unlimited 45-minute rides  
- **Annual membership:** $150 for unlimited 45-minute rides  

We also offer discounted memberships for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Visit our website to apply.

## Using the Service

**How long can I keep a bike?**  
You can ride for as long as you want, but once you go over the time included in your plan, you’ll be charged $0.15 per minute. If you’re taking a longer trip, you can dock the bike and check out another one to reset your time.

**Where can I return my bike?**  
You can return your bike to any station that has an open dock. Just push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If the station is full, check the app for the nearest station with available space—you’ll get a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**  
We don’t provide helmets, but we strongly recommend wearing one. If you’re under 16, the law requires you to wear a helmet.

**Are electric bikes available?**  
Yes. E-bikes are easy to spot because they have a green stripe. They cost an extra $0.10 per minute and provide assistance up to 20 mph.

## Safety and Problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**  
Before you ride, check the brakes, tires, and seat. If anything seems off, press the red “Report” button on the bike’s screen or report it through the app. Then return the bike to a dock so it can be taken out of service. You won’t be charged for rides under one minute.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**  
Whenever you stop, use the built-in cable lock to secure the bike. For short stops, you can also use the “Hold” feature in the app. If a bike is lost or stolen while it’s in your care, report it within 24 hours. If you don’t, you may be charged a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**  
Yes. All of our bikes have built-in front and rear lights that turn on automatically.

## Account Help

**Can I share my membership?**  
No. Memberships are for individual use only, and each account can unlock just one bike at a time. If you’re riding with a group, each person will need their own account.

**How do I cancel my membership?**  
In the app, go to Settings > Membership and choose “Cancel.” Monthly plans stay active until the end of the billing period, and annual plans are refundable within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**  
You can call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available every day from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin System

The editor has a flexible plugin system, so you can extend core functionality without changing the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin Structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a manifest file called `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines the plugin’s metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",

# The Gift of Having Nothing to Do

Last summer, my phone died while I was on a train, and I still had four hours of countryside ahead of me with nothing to do but stare out the window. For the first twenty minutes, I was nearly frantic. My hand kept reaching for my pocket the way your tongue keeps finding the spot where a tooth is missing. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored, plain and simple.

Then, somewhere along the way, something changed. Sometime after we passed a river I couldn’t have named, my mind stopped hunting for something to take in and started coming up with its own material. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn’t thought about in years. I finally worked out how to reorganize a project at work that had been bothering me for weeks. For no particular reason, I even made up an elaborate backstory for the man sleeping across the aisle. By the time we arrived at the station, I felt oddly rested, almost like I’d been away somewhere.

I think about that train ride a lot, because it showed me what I’ve been giving up. Boredom used to be part of life. It was there in waiting rooms, on long car rides, and in that empty hour between homework and dinner. Now I can erase it whenever it appears. Every spare moment can be filled with a feed, a podcast, or something to scroll through. I’ve gotten so good at avoiding boredom that I’d almost forgotten it might have a purpose.

Lately, I’ve started to think that purpose is a kind of mental housekeeping. When nothing is pulling at our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting through things. It makes connections that aren’t obvious at first. It brings up worries we’ve been outrunning and wants we haven’t fully admitted to ourselves. Psychologists have linked this kind of idle mental wandering to creativity and planning, and that fits with what I’ve experienced. My best ideas never seem to come when I’m busy consuming something. They show up in the shower, on walks, while I’m washing dishes, in those unprotected edges of the day.

Boredom can also teach us something about desire. If I stay bored long enough, I start to find out what I actually want to do instead of just reaching for whatever is being put in front of me. When I was a kid, summer boredom eventually drove me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. No one assigned me those projects. They came out of the discomfort of having an empty afternoon, and they felt like they belonged to me in a way entertainment never really does.

I don’t mean to make boredom sound romantic. It isn’t pleasant, and that’s part of the point. It’s a signal, the way hunger is a signal, that some part of us wants engagement. The problem is when we answer that signal with whatever is easiest and closest. Fast food can quiet hunger without really nourishing you, and scrolling can do the same thing to boredom, calming it without giving the mind anything meaningful to work on.

So I’ve started trying to practice a small kind of discipline. I leave my phone in my bag when I’m waiting in line. I go for walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and just watch the light change on the neighbor’s maple tree. The first few minutes always feel itchy. But then, almost every time, the restlessness opens into something roomier, and thoughts I didn’t even realize I was carrying start to rise to the surface.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I’m starting to think it’s more like fallow ground. It can look like nothing is happening, when really it’s the place where the next thing is quietly getting ready to grow.

**The Weight of a Hamburger**

When I was nine, I watched my uncle kill a pig. I was supposed to stay in the truck, and naturally, I didn’t. What stays with me isn’t the blood. It’s the silence afterward, and how quickly everything returned to normal. The men washed their hands and started talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. I remember how good it tasted, and I remember not being able to stop thinking about the pig’s eyes.

I’ve been coming back to that night for most of my adult life.

For years, I dodged the whole question the way you dodge a bill you know you may not be able to pay. I ate chicken breasts wrapped in plastic, trimmed into shapes that no longer resembled anything alive. Then I read one of those books about industrial farming—the kind clearly meant to destroy your appetite—and it did. I became a vegetarian for three years. I meant it sincerely, and I was probably a little smug about it.

What I believed then, and still believe now, is that suffering matters. Pigs are smart, social animals, and they feel fear. If I believe a dog’s pain matters, then I need to explain why a pig’s pain wouldn’t, and “because it tastes good” isn’t much of an explanation. Most of the meat people eat comes from animals raised in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them imposed on anything I loved. That’s difficult to argue with, and I’ve stopped trying.

But the certainty I had as a vegetarian has faded—not because the moral case got weaker, but because life got messier. I once spent a winter with relatives whose food came mostly from what they raised and hunted themselves, and the way they related to meat was nothing like the way I did. They knew the animals. They thanked them without irony. They wasted nothing. I couldn’t honestly say that what they were doing was worse than what I was doing while standing in a grocery store buying almond milk that had been shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating has a cost. The real question is whether you’re willing to see it.

That, uncomfortably, is where I’ve ended up. The worst thing about modern meat isn’t simply that animals die. It’s that their deaths have been hidden from us. Cruelty becomes much easier when there’s distance. If I’m going to eat an animal, I think I should be willing to know where it lived and how it died. And if I can’t bear to know that, that tells me something too.

So now I eat meat only occasionally, and I try to know where it comes from. I buy from a farmer whose fields I’ve actually walked. Sometimes I fall short. I eat whatever’s easiest at an airport or at a wedding, and I feel that old stab of discomfort. I don’t think that makes me virtuous. If anything, it may just make me a more conscious participant in something I still can’t fully defend.

I used to want a neat answer—some rule to follow, or some principle that would let me stop thinking about it. I don’t trust that desire anymore. Some questions are supposed to remain a little unsettled. They’re supposed to keep bothering you.

I still think about that pig. I don’t think the memory is telling me to stop eating meat, exactly. I think it’s asking me not to look away while I do.

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** is a highly secure seed storage facility on the Norwegian island of **Spitsbergen** in the **Svalbard archipelago**, around 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in **2008** and was created to store duplicate seed samples from gene banks across the globe, helping protect crop diversity from being lost because of war, natural disasters, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management.

The vault is built into the side of **Platåberget**, a sandstone mountain near the settlement of **Longyearbyen**. Its remote Arctic location was chosen for both political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and its naturally cold climate, along with the surrounding permafrost, helps protect the seeds even if the power fails. Inside, seeds are kept at about **−18 °C (0 °F)**, which is the standard temperature used for long-term conservation in seed banks.

Often called the world’s “**doomsday vault**,” the Svalbard Global Seed Vault is not a conventional seed bank but a backup repository. It does not own the seeds stored there. Instead, the seeds remain the property of the institutions that deposit them under a “black box” arrangement, which means only those depositors have the right to access their collections. The system is designed to support national, regional, and international gene banks by giving them an extra layer of security.

The vault was developed by the **Government of Norway** in partnership with the **Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen)** and the **Crop Trust**. It can hold millions of seed samples, covering a huge range of food crops and their wild relatives. Its collections include varieties of wheat, rice, maize, barley, beans, and many other agriculturally important species. Preserving this genetic diversity is seen as essential for future plant breeding, food security, and adapting to changing environmental conditions.

The Seed Vault has also proven its practical value. In **2015**, the **International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA)** became the first institution to withdraw seeds after conflict in Syria disrupted operations at its regional gene bank. Those seeds were used to regenerate collections and later replace them with fresh samples, showing how the vault works as a real global insurance policy for agriculture.

Since opening, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has become an international symbol of the effort to preserve biodiversity and protect the genetic foundations of the world’s food supply. It is widely considered one of the most important facilities for the long-term conservation of crop diversity.

**The Weight of Paper**

After my grandmother died, I found a shoebox full of her letters, bundled by year with rubber bands. Mine were there too: earnest childhood notes about school and a lost tooth, which she had kept for decades. But I couldn’t stop reading her letters, the ones my mother had saved and eventually passed on to me.

Nothing much happens in them. The tomatoes are ripening late. Mrs. Dolan’s hip still isn’t any better. It rained on Tuesday, then again on Wednesday, and then, she wrote, “it seemed to lose interest.” I laughed out loud, standing alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry wit in that slanted blue ink. In one place she had crossed out a word and written a different one above it, and I could almost see the moment she paused and changed her mind. That tiny correction told me more about her than any photograph could.

I think that’s what we lose when we stop writing letters: not information, but evidence of attention. A letter proves that someone sat down and kept you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes. They weren’t doing it while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. They chose a page, a pen, and you. I send dozens of messages a day now, and they’re quick and kind and practical, but they’re also weightless. They arrive in the middle of distraction and get answered in the middle of distraction. Almost none of them are saved. How could they be?

Letters also demanded a kind of patience that shaped what people were able to say. You couldn’t send off a feeling and take it back ten seconds later. You had to let a thought run its course, and sometimes by the time it did, it had changed. From the shoebox I learned that my grandfather once wrote my grandmother a three-page letter about a quarrel, and by the last paragraph he was contradicting the first. He hadn’t intended to forgive her when he started writing. The letter carried him there. A text would probably have kept him angry, or reduced the whole argument to a single clipped word.

And then there was the waiting. Now we treat waiting as nothing but a cost, a problem to be solved by engineering it away. But the space between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox carrying a small, private hope. And when something finally arrived, it had made a journey to get to you. It bore a stamp, a smudge, the faint smell of someone else’s house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took me an hour and a half, much longer than I expected, because I kept uncovering things I hadn’t known I wanted to say. My handwriting had grown ragged from disuse. I crossed out one word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope into the mailbox, I felt strangely exposed, as if I had handed over something I could no longer revise.

She wrote back three weeks later. I still have her letter on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. In it, among other things, she says that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
This proposal outlines a caching layer for the web API aimed at reducing response latency, lowering backend load, and improving scalability. The cache would store frequently requested API responses so they can be served without repeatedly calling the database or downstream services.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Maintain acceptable data freshness
- Provide observability into cache behavior

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data for all endpoints

## Architecture
The caching layer would sit between the API application and the backend data sources. For each request, the API would first check the cache for a stored response. If a valid cached entry is found, it would be returned right away. If not, the API would fetch the data from the source, return the response, and then write it to the cache.

A distributed in-memory store like Redis is the recommended choice because it offers low latency, built-in expiration support, and strong operational maturity. For static or public GET endpoints, a CDN or edge cache could also be added later.

## Cache Strategy
The initial implementation would use a **cache-aside** approach:

1. A client requests a resource
2. The API looks up the cache key
3. If there is a hit, it returns the cached response
4. If there is a miss, it fetches the data from the backend
5. It stores the result in the cache with a TTL
6. It returns the response

This strategy is straightforward, explicit, and well suited to read-heavy workloads.

## Key Design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context, such as locale

Example:  
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item should have a TTL based on how often the endpoint changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Cache invalidation should happen when writes affect cached resources. For example, if a product is updated, the related product detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. In cases where exact invalidation is difficult, shorter TTLs should be used instead.

## Reliability Considerations
To prevent cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Negative caching can also be used briefly for known missing resources to reduce repeated misses. If the cache becomes unavailable, the API must gracefully fall back to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches should exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Metrics should include:

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
This proposal outlines a caching layer for the web API aimed at reducing response latency, lowering backend load, and improving scalability. The cache would store frequently requested API responses so they can be served without repeatedly calling the database or downstream services.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Maintain acceptable data freshness
- Provide observability into cache behavior

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data for all endpoints

## Architecture
The caching layer would sit between the API application and the backend data sources. For each request, the API would first check the cache for a stored response. If a valid cached entry is found, it would be returned right away. If not, the API would fetch the data from the source, return the response, and then write it to the cache.

A distributed in-memory store like Redis is the recommended choice because it offers low latency, built-in expiration support, and strong operational maturity. For static or public GET endpoints, a CDN or edge cache could also be added later.

## Cache Strategy
The initial implementation would use a **cache-aside** approach:

1. A client requests a resource
2. The API looks up the cache key
3. If there is a hit, it returns the cached response
4. If there is a miss, it fetches the data from the backend
5. It stores the result in the cache with a TTL
6. It returns the response

This strategy is straightforward, explicit, and well suited to read-heavy workloads.

## Key Design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context, such as locale

Example:  
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item should have a TTL based on how often the endpoint changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Cache invalidation should happen when writes affect cached resources. For example, if a product is updated, the related product detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. In cases where exact invalidation is difficult, shorter TTLs should be used instead.

## Reliability Considerations
To prevent cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Negative caching can also be used briefly for known missing resources to reduce repeated misses. If the cache becomes unavailable, the API must gracefully fall back to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches should exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Metrics should include:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Backend request reduction

Structured logs and dashboards should also be added to help monitor effectiveness.

## Rollout Plan
The rollout should begin with a small group of high-read, low-volatility GET endpoints. After measuring hit rate and latency improvements, the cache can be expanded gradually. This phased approach helps minimize risk while confirming real-world impact.

The Library of Alexandria was one of the most famous libraries of the ancient world and a major center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was connected to the Mouseion, or “Temple of the Muses,” a research institution established under the Ptolemaic dynasty after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Even though many details about it are still uncertain, the library has become a lasting symbol of learning, intellectual ambition, and cultural loss.

It was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, most likely during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to become the leading center of Greek culture and scholarship, so they collected texts from across the Mediterranean world, including works on literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe these efforts as especially aggressive: books brought into the city were reportedly copied, and in some cases the originals were kept for the library while copies were returned to their owners.

The Library of Alexandria was not just a place where scrolls were stored. It was part of a larger scholarly community where resident scholars studied, edited, and compared texts, helping produce critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. The institution drew prominent intellectuals, including Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a massive bibliographic catalogue often considered one of the earliest library catalogues in history.

Estimates of the library’s size vary widely, with ancient and modern figures ranging from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Scholars also continue to debate exactly how the library was organized and how the main library was related to a possible “daughter library” in the Serapeum.

The destruction of the Library of Alexandria is one of the most famous stories in cultural history, but it probably was not the result of a single catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources link its decline to several different episodes, including Julius Caesar’s campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil during the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially in the 4th century CE. Most modern historians think the library declined gradually over centuries rather than being wiped out all at once.

The library’s legacy has lasted far beyond antiquity. It has come to stand for both the ideal of universal knowledge and the fragility of cultural memory. In modern Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, inaugurated in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution and to its enduring place in world history.
