# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League**, or simply the **Hansa**, was a commercial and defensive alliance of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It began in the 12th century and reached its peak between the 13th and 15th centuries, when it dominated trade in the Baltic Sea and North Sea regions. Most of its member cities were located along the coasts of what are now Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and nearby areas.

## Origins

The League grew out of groups of German merchants who traveled together for safety from piracy and banditry. A key turning point was the founding of Lübeck in 1143 and its rise as a gateway to the Baltic. Lübeck’s alliance with Hamburg in 1241 is often seen as an early milestone. Over time, many other towns joined as well, including Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was never a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, no permanent treasury, and no formal constitution. Instead, it operated as a loose association whose members met in periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, held mainly in Lübeck. Its decisions were carried out through collective economic pressure, such as trade embargoes, and sometimes through military action. Lübeck is generally considered the League’s leading city and was often called its “Queen.”

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants dealt mainly in bulk goods. From the east they brought timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye. From the west and south they carried cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also essential to this trade. The League maintained major overseas trading posts, known as *Kontore*, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves had special privileges and operated according to their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa’s power led to conflicts with rulers who resented its trading privileges. The most important of these was its war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later on, growing competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants gradually weakened its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century onward, the League declined for several reasons. Stronger territorial states emerged, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power expanded, and internal divisions grew. The loss of important privileges also hurt the League, including the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598. The last formal assembly was held in 1669, although Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries afterward.

## Legacy

The League left a lasting architectural and cultural mark, especially through the brick Gothic buildings found across the Baltic region. Hamburg and Bremen still include “Free and Hanseatic City” in their official titles. Today, the “New Hanse” and the annual Hanseatic Days continue to celebrate that heritage.

The Dust Bowl was a time of severe dust storms and environmental disaster that hit the Great Plains of the United States during the 1930s, especially from 1934 to 1936. It happened because of a mix of prolonged drought, strong winds, and poor farming practices that left the soil exposed to erosion. The damage was enormous environmentally, economically, and socially, especially in Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico.

Before the Dust Bowl, much of the Great Plains was covered with deep-rooted native grasses that held the soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large stretches of prairie were plowed up for wheat farming and cattle grazing. Driven by high crop prices and the belief that “rain follows the plow,” many farmers pushed cultivation into marginal land. When drought arrived in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil dried out and was easily swept away by high winds.

Dust storms became one of the most recognizable features of the era. Sometimes called “black blizzards,” these storms carried huge clouds of soil over towns, farms, and even faraway cities. One of the most famous storms struck on April 14, 1935, a day known as Black Sunday, when a massive wall of dust moved across the southern Plains. The storms ruined crops, buried machinery, killed livestock, and caused widespread breathing problems known as “dust pneumonia.”

The Dust Bowl made the suffering of the Great Depression even worse. Farm incomes collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas, and headed to California and other western states in search of jobs and better living conditions. These migrants were often called “Okies,” although many were not actually from Oklahoma. Their experiences were later portrayed in works like John Steinbeck’s *The Grapes of Wrath*.

The federal government responded with a variety of relief and conservation efforts under President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal. In 1935, the Soil Conservation Service was created to encourage farming methods that reduced erosion, including contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and planting shelterbelts of trees. Aid programs also helped struggling farm families either relocate or stay on their land.

Rain gradually returned to the Plains in the late 1930s, which eased the worst of the crisis. The Dust Bowl is still considered one of the most important environmental disasters in U.S. history. It is often used as a warning about the dangers of unsustainable land use, climate extremes, and how vulnerable agricultural systems can be to ecological change.

# The Friendship I Carry Around in My Pocket

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country, and we started writing letters. They were messy, with crossed-out words and little drawings in the margins. Sometimes it took two weeks for a reply, sometimes three. I still remember the small excitement of spotting her handwriting in the mailbox, and how I reread those letters so many times the folds started to soften. Within a year, we’d lost touch. Back then, that’s just what distance did.

My kids will probably never experience that kind of loss, and I’m not sure yet how I feel about that.

I notice how much social media has changed friendship most when I try to put it into words. I know what my college roommate ate for dinner last night. I know her daughter just lost a tooth, that her mother has been sick, and that she’s unhappy at work. I haven’t actually talked to her in four years. Is she still my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one, she’s someone I “keep up with,” which is its own odd category: closeness without contact, intimacy without conversation.

There’s something genuinely valuable in that. I’ve seen friendships make it through moves, career shifts, and the slow drifting apart that used to end them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I reply while I’m doing the dishes. It’s not the same as sitting together in person, but it’s not nothing either. It’s a thread, and threads can be tightened again. When we do finally meet up, we’re not starting from scratch.

But the downsides are quieter, and I’ve felt them more the older I get. Social media can make friendship feel performative, like there’s always an audience. I’ve caught myself shaping a moment before I’ve fully lived it—tilting the dinner table for a better photo, thinking up a caption while a friend is still talking. The moment turns into content, and the friend becomes, at least a little, part of the cast.

It’s also made affection feel cheap. A like costs nothing. A birthday message prompted by a platform reminder takes four seconds. We send these tiny signals and convince ourselves we’ve done the work of caring, even though real friendship has always asked for something slower and less efficient: showing up, sitting through the awkward silence, driving across town when someone’s life is falling apart. No app has automated that, even if it sometimes makes us feel like it has.

Last winter, a friend I’d only been “liking” from a distance posted something vague and sad. I almost kept scrolling. Instead, I called her. We talked for two hours. She cried, and I realized how long it had been since I’d heard her actual voice. The post was a small flare, and I’d almost mistaken it for part of the background.

That’s where I’ve landed. Social media hasn’t ruined friendship, and it hasn’t perfected it either. It’s widened the net and thinned the rope. What happens with that slack is up to us. We can treat the feed as the friendship, or we can treat it as a doorway into one.

I still have my friend’s old letters, softened at the folds. I don’t want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I do miss writing that way—slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon, I usually start to notice a weird shift around the office. Everyone is still doing the usual things—answering emails, sitting through meetings, updating spreadsheets—but the energy is different. The edge that was there on Monday has faded. Conversations wander. Little tasks take longer than they should. By Friday, it can feel like people are acting out the idea of working rather than actually getting much done. That feeling has made me more and more sympathetic to the argument for a four-day work week.

What convinces me most is not just the nice idea of having another morning to sleep in, appealing as that is. It is the growing realization that more time spent at work does not automatically lead to better work. In a lot of jobs, especially office jobs, productivity is not just about the number of hours people put in. Attention runs out. Creativity wears down when it is pushed too hard. Tired people make worse decisions. We often talk as if stamina is the ultimate professional virtue, but in reality, clear thinking matters more than simply lasting longer. A shorter week recognizes something fundamentally human: people are not machines, and acting like they are usually produces mediocre results.

I also find the four-day week appealing because it treats rest as something worthwhile instead of something self-indulgent. In a lot of work cultures, being exhausted is almost treated like a badge of honor. If you are overwhelmed, that means you must be important; if you are unavailable, that means you are needed. But that way of thinking feels emptier and emptier to me. Rest is not the opposite of responsibility. It is one of the things that makes responsibility possible. An extra day away from work can mean time to recover, to take care of children or parents, to go to a doctor’s appointment without stress, to read, to exercise, to be a person outside the constant demands of employers and inboxes. When people have the space to live fuller lives, they often come back to work more focused and less resentful.

I think there is also a moral case for the four-day work week. For generations, we have been told that technological progress would bring efficiency and freedom. But for many workers, those gains have not turned into more leisure; they have just led to higher expectations. We can answer messages immediately, create documents more quickly, and automate routine tasks, yet the payoff is often just more work. A four-day week points to another possibility: that the benefits of innovation could finally be shared as time. And time, after all, is one of the most valuable resources anyone has.

Of course, not every profession can switch to the same schedule in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service industries all face real practical constraints. A four-day work week is not some magical solution to every workplace problem. It takes careful planning, staffing changes, and a real commitment not to squeeze five days’ worth of meetings into four. But the fact that there are challenges does not undermine the core idea. If anything, it makes the need to question old assumptions even clearer.

To me, the argument for a four-day work week is really an argument about dignity. It asks whether work is supposed to take the best parts of our lives or help sustain them. I do not think people want to contribute less. I think they want to contribute in a way that is sustainable and still have enough of themselves left for the rest of life.

A fast-moving wildfire tore through dry timber along the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing more than 3,000 residents to evacuate and leading officials to close the park to all visitors.

The fire, called the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and has since burned an estimated 14,000 acres. As of Wednesday morning, fire officials said it was 0% contained.

“This fire is moving faster than anything we’ve seen in this area in a decade,” Incident Commander Dana Whitfield said at an evening briefing. “Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us.”

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for the communities of Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. Another 2,000 residents in nearby areas were told to be ready to leave at a moment’s notice. Sheriff’s deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones across the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with little more than their pets and medications.

“We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could,” said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who evacuated with her two children and their dog. “I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back.”

# The Weight of Boxes

The first thing I noticed about my new city was how loud the quiet felt. In my old apartment, I knew every sound by heart: the radiator knocking, the upstairs neighbor’s heavy footsteps, the bus groaning past at 6:40 every morning. Here, in a sublet that carried the faint smell of someone else’s cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn’t even identify.

No one really tells you that moving feels a little like choosing amnesia. You give up your fluency. I’d spent nine years in my old city, long enough to move through it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had the good tomatoes, which streets flooded in the spring, which barista would start making my order the moment I walked in. In the new city, I got lost on the way to the pharmacy. I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, completely stalled by brands I didn’t recognize. At thirty-four, it was both humbling and slightly ridiculous to feel that childlike.

But that humbling feeling is part of the gift, too. Within a week, my attention had sharpened in a way it hadn’t in years. I started noticing the brick on my street, that warm rust color that seemed to glow at dusk. I noticed that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere, mostly because I didn’t have a short way yet. A city you don’t know forces you to actually see it, and I realized that seeing—really looking—is a kind of pleasure I’d stopped making room for. Routine had quietly worn my days smooth until they all felt interchangeable.

There were smaller pleasures too. I found a bakery where the owner started setting aside the end pieces of the rye loaf for me. I discovered a river path where, on Sunday mornings, runners and old men holding fishing rods occupied the same narrow stretch of asphalt in easy, peaceful disregard for each other. Every discovery felt oddly private, like treasure, because no one had pointed me toward it. I’d found it by wandering.

Still, the losses were real, and they showed up on their own timetable. They arrived on a Tuesday, when something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, only to do the time-zone math and set it back down. They arrived in the quiet of the second month, after the novelty had worn thin and I had to admit that friendship can’t be unpacked the way boxes can. It builds slowly—through repetition, through accident, through simply being there. I had exchanged people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that turned out to be lonelier than I expected.

I’ve been here a year now. The bus no longer sounds unfamiliar. I have a place for tomatoes. Last month, the woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I realized I actually had a week worth talking about. I still miss the old city, in the way you miss a language you once spoke fluently.

But I’ve started to think homesickness is just the cost of having loved a place, and paying that cost doesn’t mean you made the wrong choice. Moving taught me that I could be remade, that I was more portable than I’d imagined. The boxes have been gone for a long time. What I was carrying, it turns out, was never inside them.

The Dust Bowl, often called the Dirty Thirties, was a period in the 1930s when severe dust storms caused major ecological and agricultural damage across the prairie lands of the United States and Canada. It happened because a severe drought hit after decades of widespread farming that had not used methods to protect the soil from wind erosion, such as crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large numbers of settlers moved onto the Great Plains, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by an unusually wet period in the early 1900s. Farmers plowed under the native deep-rooted prairie grasses to plant wheat. High wheat prices during and after World War I sped up this expansion, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines made it possible to farm much more land than before. As a result, millions of acres of grassland were turned into cropland, leaving the soil exposed.

A series of droughts began in 1930 and came back in waves through 1936 and again in 1939–1940. With the grasses that had once held the soil in place gone, strong winds lifted the dry topsoil into huge dust clouds. The hardest-hit area included the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles, along with parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

One of the most infamous storms struck on April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, when a massive dust storm swept across the southern plains and turned daytime into darkness. The next day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term “Dust Bowl” in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some of these storms carried dust all the way to Washington, D.C., and even to ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

The storms ruined crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many people developed “dust pneumonia” and other respiratory illnesses. At the same time, the Great Depression was making life even harder, and together these crises forced many families off their farms. About 3.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s, many of them heading to California. Their experiences were later captured in works like John Steinbeck’s 1939 novel *The Grapes of Wrath*, Dorothea Lange’s photographs, and Woody Guthrie’s songs.

The federal government responded by creating programs to deal with the crisis. In 1935, under Hugh Hammond Bennett, the Soil Conservation Service was established and encouraged soil-saving practices such as contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, which began in 1934, planted millions of trees in windbreaks, or shelterbelts, across the Plains. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also placed regulations on grazing on public lands.

Rain returned in late 1939, bringing the drought to an end. The Dust Bowl is still remembered as one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, and it had a lasting influence on modern soil conservation policy and agricultural practices.

The Erie Canal is a historic canal in New York State that played a huge role in the economic development of the United States during the 19th century. When it opened in 1825, it created a navigable water route between the Hudson River at Albany and Lake Erie at Buffalo, effectively linking the Atlantic Ocean with the Great Lakes. This dramatically lowered transportation costs, sped up westward settlement, and helped make New York City the nation’s leading port.

The idea for the canal emerged in the early 19th century as a way to solve the problem of moving goods and people across the Appalachian barrier. At the time, overland travel was slow, costly, and often unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became the project’s strongest political supporter, though critics mockingly referred to it as “Clinton’s Ditch.” Construction began in 1817 and required the labor of thousands of workers, including many immigrants, who cleared forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks through difficult terrain.

By the time it was finished, the original Erie Canal stretched about 363 miles (584 km), measured 40 feet (12 m) wide, and was 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. It had 83 locks, which enabled boats to handle a total elevation change of more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. To mark the occasion, Governor Clinton staged the “Wedding of the Waters,” a ceremonial trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor during which water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic Ocean.

The Erie Canal quickly became one of the most important transportation routes in North America. Shipping costs between the Midwest and the East Coast dropped sharply, making it much cheaper to move agricultural products, raw materials, and manufactured goods. Communities along the canal, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, expanded rapidly. The canal also encouraged migration into western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

Because it was so successful, the canal was expanded several times during the 19th century. In the early 20th century, much of its original route became part of the larger New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918 and combined canalized rivers with newly dug canal sections. Although railroads and highways eventually diminished its commercial importance, the Erie Canal remained a powerful symbol of American engineering and ambition.

Today, the Erie Canal is used mostly for recreation, tourism, and heritage purposes. It continues to be recognized as a landmark in the history of transportation, commerce, and the expansion of the United States.

Learning a second language as an adult taught me that intelligence is a much humbler thing than I once believed. Before I began, I pictured language learning as a test of memory, discipline, and maybe even talent. I assumed that if I worked hard enough, I would move steadily from confusion to fluency, picking up grammar rules and vocabulary the way someone gathers tools. Instead, it felt much more like learning how to be a beginner again.

As a child, I never noticed how much of life is shaped by language. I moved through my first language without thinking. I joked, apologized, complained, and told stories as naturally as breathing. But when I started learning another language as an adult, even the simplest interactions suddenly felt heavy. I could have a thought in my mind in full color and then realize I only had the words to express it in black and white. A personality that felt articulate and quick in one language became hesitant and reduced in another. It was startling to see how much of what I thought of as “myself” depended on being able to express myself easily.

That experience made me more patient, not just with myself but with other people too. When you struggle to ask where the bathroom is, accidentally order the wrong food, or misunderstand a question and answer confidently anyway, you start to see human communication more generously. I became more aware of how brave people are every day when they live, work, and raise families in a language that is not fully theirs. Before learning a second language, I admired bilingualism in an abstract way. Afterward, I understood it as a form of daily courage.

It also taught me that embarrassment is something you can survive. Adults often avoid learning experiences that make them look foolish. Children, because they have no choice, are constantly corrected, misunderstood, and exposed, and they keep going anyway. Adults, by contrast, guard competence as if it were fragile. Learning another language forced me to speak badly, mispronounce things, forget words I had “already learned,” and confront the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first, that was frustrating. Eventually, it became freeing. I realized that improvement depends less on avoiding mistakes than on being willing to endure them.

Maybe most unexpectedly, learning a second language changed the way I listen. In my native language, I often listen only for meaning. In a second language, I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention. I pay attention to what is said, what is implied, and what I may have missed. That way of listening started to carry over into my first language too. I became slower to assume, quicker to ask, and more aware that understanding another person is never quite as automatic as it seems.

Learning a second language as an adult did not just give me another way to speak. It changed how I think about fluency, identity, and patience. It taught me that growth is often awkward, that humility can be useful, and that communication is both more fragile and more generous than I once understood. More than anything, it reminded me that becoming a beginner again is not a return to weakness. It is a return to attention.

A record number of voters showed up Tuesday for the Riverton School Board election, a sign of unusually strong public interest in a race that usually gets little attention outside education circles.

The Riverton County Elections Office said more than 18,400 ballots were cast, which amounts to about 46 percent of the district’s registered voters. Officials said that made it the highest turnout ever for a stand-alone school-board election in the community, beating the previous record set in 2017 by nearly 5,000 votes.

Election workers said lines stayed steady all day at polling places across the district, with the biggest crowds in the morning and again after work. Early voting and absentee ballots also rose sharply and helped drive the historic turnout.

“This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see,” said County Elections Director Marisol Vega. “School-board elections typically bring in a smaller slice of the electorate, so this level of turnout is remarkable.”

The surge in interest came after months of public debate over school funding, overcrowded classrooms, campus safety, and the future of the district’s curriculum. Candidate forums attracted large crowds, and community groups on all sides ran major outreach efforts encouraging residents to vote.

Three seats were open in the race. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his seat, and newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace appeared on track to win based on unofficial returns released Tuesday night. Final certified results are expected later this week, though observers said the margins were large enough that the outcome was unlikely to change.

Backers of the apparent winners said the results sent a clear message that the district wants both stability and new ideas. “People care deeply about what happens in our schools,” Gomez told supporters at a gathering Tuesday evening. “Tonight’s turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families.”

Not everyone agreed on what the results meant, but many residents said the turnout itself was encouraging. Parents, teachers, and retirees interviewed outside polling places said they shared a belief that the school board has an outsized effect on everyday life, from academic standards to bus routes and extracurricular programs.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the election showed how invested the public is in the district’s future. “Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate,” Liu said. “That kind of involvement strengthens public education.”

Local analysts said the turnout could change the way future elections unfold, showing that school-board races can motivate voters when the issues feel immediate and personal. For Riverton, Tuesday’s results brought not just new leadership, but also a striking display of democratic participation.

VoltNest Energy, a fast-growing home energy startup, has voluntarily recalled one of its residential battery systems after reports that a defect could cause the unit to overheat, raising concerns about a possible fire risk in homes where it was installed.

On Tuesday, the company said it is recalling about 8,200 units of its PowerVault S1 battery, a wall-mounted system built to store electricity from rooftop solar panels or provide backup power during outages. The affected batteries were sold in the United States between March 2024 and September 2026 through solar installers and on the company’s website.

In a statement, VoltNest said it had received 27 reports of overheating. Five of those incidents involved minor property damage, including scorched walls and melted wiring insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though the company said two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

According to the startup, the problem appears to be tied to a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules supplied by a third-party vendor. The company said that under certain charging conditions, an internal component can fail and potentially cause excessive heat buildup.

“We are acting out of an abundance of caution,” VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. “Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible.”

Customers are being told to shut down the battery immediately using the system’s main disconnect switch and not to try repairing or removing it themselves. VoltNest said it will offer free inspections, software diagnostics and replacements where needed. The company has also released a firmware update meant to reduce charging stress while replacement plans move forward, but it stressed that the software patch is not a substitute for the recall.

The recall was announced in coordination with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, which urged owners to follow the shutdown instructions and contact VoltNest or their installer. The agency said recalled units can be identified by serial numbers starting with PVS1-24 and PVS1-25.

The episode is a major test for VoltNest, a venture-backed startup that has marketed itself as a lower-cost competitor in the rapidly growing home battery market. Founded in 2021, the company has expanded quickly as demand for residential backup power has risen alongside more frequent extreme weather and increasing strain on electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could temporarily slow the company’s momentum, but that its response may matter more than the defect itself.

“Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand,” said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. “But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms.”

VoltNest Energy, a fast-growing home energy startup, has voluntarily recalled one of its residential battery systems after reports that a defect could cause the unit to overheat, raising concerns about a possible fire risk in homes where it was installed.

On Tuesday, the company said it is recalling about 8,200 units of its PowerVault S1 battery, a wall-mounted system built to store electricity from rooftop solar panels or provide backup power during outages. The affected batteries were sold in the United States between March 2024 and September 2026 through solar installers and on the company’s website.

In a statement, VoltNest said it had received 27 reports of overheating. Five of those incidents involved minor property damage, including scorched walls and melted wiring insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though the company said two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

According to the startup, the problem appears to be tied to a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules supplied by a third-party vendor. The company said that under certain charging conditions, an internal component can fail and potentially cause excessive heat buildup.

“We are acting out of an abundance of caution,” VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. “Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible.”

Customers are being told to shut down the battery immediately using the system’s main disconnect switch and not to try repairing or removing it themselves. VoltNest said it will offer free inspections, software diagnostics and replacements where needed. The company has also released a firmware update meant to reduce charging stress while replacement plans move forward, but it stressed that the software patch is not a substitute for the recall.

The recall was announced in coordination with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, which urged owners to follow the shutdown instructions and contact VoltNest or their installer. The agency said recalled units can be identified by serial numbers starting with PVS1-24 and PVS1-25.

The episode is a major test for VoltNest, a venture-backed startup that has marketed itself as a lower-cost competitor in the rapidly growing home battery market. Founded in 2021, the company has expanded quickly as demand for residential backup power has risen alongside more frequent extreme weather and increasing strain on electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could temporarily slow the company’s momentum, but that its response may matter more than the defect itself.

“Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand,” said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. “But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms.”

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (Norwegian: *Svalbard globale frøhvelv*) is a highly secure backup facility for the world’s crop diversity on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago. In the media, it is often referred to as the “Doomsday Vault.” Its purpose is to store duplicate seed samples from gene banks around the world, providing insurance against the loss of collections due to accidents, mismanagement, war, or natural disasters.

## History

The idea for the vault was first proposed in the 1980s and later gained momentum through the efforts of agricultural scientist Cary Fowler, who went on to lead the Global Crop Diversity Trust, now known as the Crop Trust. Construction was funded by the Norwegian government at a cost of about NOK 50 million, and the facility officially opened on 26 February 2008.

## Location and design

The vault is built inside a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen, around 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole, at roughly 130 metres above sea level. That elevation was chosen so the facility would remain above any projected sea-level rise. A tunnel approximately 120 metres long leads to three storage chambers, and each chamber is designed to hold up to 1.5 million seed samples. Altogether, the vault has the capacity for 4.5 million varieties, equal to about 2.25 billion seeds.

The surrounding permafrost helps provide natural cooling, while refrigeration keeps the chambers at about −18 °C, the standard temperature for long-term seed storage. In those cold, low-moisture conditions, seeds from many major crops can remain viable for centuries or even longer. The site was also chosen because of its geological stability and low tectonic activity.

## Operation

The vault is owned by the Norwegian government and operated in cooperation with the Crop Trust and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen). Storage is free, with the costs covered by Norway and the Crop Trust. Institutions that deposit seeds keep ownership of their samples, which are sealed in foil packages and stored in boxes that no one else is allowed to open. The vault serves only as a backup, and only the depositors can withdraw their material.

By the early 2020s, the collection included more than 1.2 million samples from nearly every country, covering varieties of rice, wheat, maize, barley, sorghum, and many regional crops.

## Notable events

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first major withdrawal. It requested copies of seeds that had originally been stored in Aleppo, Syria, after the Syrian civil war disrupted its gene bank operations. Those seeds were then used to rebuild collections in Morocco and Lebanon.

In 2017, unusually warm weather combined with heavy rain caused meltwater to enter the entrance tunnel. The seeds themselves were not affected, but Norway later funded major upgrades, including waterproofing and improved drainage.

## Significance

The vault stands as a symbol of international cooperation in food security and biodiversity conservation. At the same time, it illustrates how climate change can pose risks even to facilities specifically designed to endure long-term threats.

I’ve never really trusted habits that show up with a lot of ceremony. The ones that actually help me are usually small and almost modest: making coffee before I’m fully awake, cracking open a window even in winter, going for a walk for no particular reason. Of all of them, walking is the one I’ve come to rely on most. It asks the least from me and gives the most back.

I didn’t always think of walking as something meaningful. For a long time, it was just what happened between one place and another. It belonged to errands, missed buses, parking a couple of streets away, trudging across campus in bad weather. It was practical, easy to overlook, and often a little irritating. But somewhere along the line, it shifted. It stopped feeling like a delay before life started and became a way of stepping into life itself.

Part of what makes it comforting is how unremarkable it is. Walking doesn’t require talent, expensive gear, or even the right frame of mind. It doesn’t ask me to become a better version of myself. On days when I’m tired, restless, or carrying that vague modern dissatisfaction—too much screen time, too many tabs open in my head—I can still put on shoes and head outside. That simplicity feels almost like a correction. So much of modern life is frictionless in exactly the wrong ways: messages arrive instantly, news trails me from room to room, whole afternoons vanish while my body stays still. Walking brings back a kind of friction that is actually useful. It reminds me that distance is real, weather is real, and my legs are real.

I’ve noticed my thoughts act differently when I’m walking. At a desk, problems tend to stiffen. They take on that dense, stale feeling of something I’ve handled too much. But on a walk, even the worries I know by heart begin to loosen. The rhythm of my steps gives my mind just enough to do that it stops clutching so hard. I’ve had ideas come to me while crossing the street, remembered lines I was sure I’d lost, softened a little toward other people, softened a little toward myself. None of it feels mystical. It’s just that movement changes the size of a thought. What feels inescapable indoors becomes, outside, just one thing among many: a barking dog, a train going by, the smell of freshly cut grass, the sudden authority of a tree.

Walking also brings me back to my senses in the most literal way. I start noticing the world not as scenery but as company. The same street is never really the same street twice. The seasons keep editing it: wet leaves stuck to the sidewalk, the medicinal brightness of cold air, the worn-out abundance of late summer gardens. There are also the small neighborhood dramas: a child drawing suns in chalk on the pavement, someone wobbling through learning to ride a bike, a curtain lifted and let fall. To walk regularly is to become a quiet kind of witness. You start to learn the habits of dogs, the timing of sprinklers, the spots where the first crocuses stubbornly appear. Familiarity builds, and with it comes a gentle affection.

What I value most, though, is that walking offers a kind of progress that can’t be optimized until it becomes meaningless. One foot in front of the other is both a set of directions and a philosophy. You don’t have to leap. You don’t have to finish everything today. You move, you stop, you keep going. There’s humility in that, and there’s relief too.

When I come back from a walk, my life is usually the same in any measurable sense. The emails are still waiting, and so are the unanswered questions. But I feel a little more reassembled. I’m reminded that the world is larger than whatever has been occupying me, and that I can meet it with my own body, at a human pace. For something so ordinary, walking has a remarkable power: it restores my sense of proportion. And more and more, that feels like a kind of grace.

To create a new event on a user’s calendar, send a `POST` request to `/v1/events`.

This endpoint lets you create a calendar event with a title, start time, and end time. You can also optionally include a description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and a time zone. If the request succeeds, the API returns the newly created event object, including its unique identifier.

Authentication is required. Include a valid bearer token in the request:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

You’ll also need these request headers:

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

Here’s an example request body:

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

The request body supports these fields:

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title, max 200 characters |
| start | string | Yes | Start date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| end | string | Yes | End date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| description | string | No | Event details, max 5000 characters |
| location | string | No | Event location |
| timezone | string | No | IANA time zone, e.g. `America/New_York` |
| attendees | array[string] | No | List of attendee email addresses |
| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder definitions |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |
| reminders[].minutesBefore | integer | Yes | Minutes before event start |
| recurrence | object | No | Recurrence settings |
| recurrence.frequency | string | No | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or `yearly` |
| recurrence.interval | integer | No | Repeat interval, must be greater than 0 |

A successful response returns `201 Created`, along with the new event object:

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01J9X8K7M2R4A6P9",
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "status": "confirmed",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-10T14:22:31Z"
}
```

Possible error responses include:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 400 Bad Request | Missing required fields, invalid JSON, or malformed dates |
| 401 Unauthorized | Missing or invalid access token |
| 403 Forbidden | Token does not have permission to create events |
| 409 Conflict | Event overlaps with a protected calendar block |
| 422 Unprocessable Entity | Validation failed, such as `end` occurring before `start` |

Example error response:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "The `end` time must be later than `start`."
  }
}
```

A few things to keep in mind:

- All timestamps must use ISO 8601 format.
- If `timezone` is omitted, the calendar’s default time zone is used.
- Attendees may receive invitations depending on account settings.
- Recurring events may create a series rather than a single standalone event.

Riverbend Health, a regional system with seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, said Tuesday that hackers got into its systems and may have taken personal and medical information belonging to about 378,000 current and former patients.

The Ohio-based network said in a statement on its website that it discovered suspicious activity on March 4, after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used for billing records. Investigators believe the attackers may have been inside the system since mid-February, meaning they could have had access for roughly three weeks.

“We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients,” said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health’s chief executive. “Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again.”

Riverbend said the exposed information may include names, dates of birth, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details about diagnoses and treatments. The network said it has found no evidence that the attackers reached its electronic health record system, which contains full clinical charts, but emphasized that the investigation is still underway.

Emergency departments stayed open during the incident, but Riverbend said some scheduling and billing systems were offline for nearly a week. Several patients said appointments were rescheduled and test results were delayed.

“I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper,” said Dana Whitfield, 54, who gets care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. “Now I’m worried about who has my information.”

Riverbend said it has brought in an outside cybersecurity firm and notified both the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which keeps a public list of major health care breaches. The network said it has not received a ransom demand, although a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is reviewing those claims.

Security experts say health care organizations continue to be attractive targets because medical records contain a valuable combination of information that can be used for identity theft and fraud.

“A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes. A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years,” said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant who is not involved in the investigation.

Riverbend said it will start mailing notification letters next week and will offer two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. Patients can call a dedicated hotline at 1-800-555-0142.

The network also urged patients to review insurance statements for any unfamiliar services and to consider placing fraud alerts on their credit files.

Note: This article is a fictional work created for illustrative purposes.

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, often considered the earliest known analog computer. It was used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades ahead of time, and to follow the cycles of the Greek calendar, including the dates of major Panhellenic games. The device is generally dated to the 2nd or 1st century BCE.

It was recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. Sponge divers first discovered the wreck in 1900, and salvage operations led by the Greek Navy and archaeologists brought up statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. That lump was later shown to contain gears and inscriptions. Today, the mechanism is held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

The device was enclosed in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its bronze parts, many of them thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. When a crank was turned, it drove a system of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, moving pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

On the front dial, the mechanism showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac along with a calendar. The Moon’s phase appeared by means of a small rotating, partly silvered ball. On the back were two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle, which lasts 19 years and matches solar years to lunar months, and one for the Saros cycle, which lasts about 18 years and was used to predict eclipses. Smaller subsidiary dials tracked additional cycles, including the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

The Moon’s irregular motion, caused by its elliptical orbit, was modeled through a pin-and-slot mechanism that used two gears with offset axes. This reflects the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

Early studies by Valerios Stais, and later by Derek de Solla Price in the 1950s through the 1970s, established the mechanism’s basic function. X-ray imaging in the 1970s, followed by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which began in 2005, used microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging to read much of the inscriptions, which amount to a user’s manual. Researchers have also suggested that the device displayed planetary positions, and reconstructions of that kind of gearing have been published, though the evidence is still incomplete.

The sophistication of the mechanism has no known parallel among surviving artifacts for more than a thousand years, until the appearance of medieval astronomical clocks in Europe and the Islamic world. Its origin is still debated, with possible links to Rhodes, Corinth, or Syracuse, and to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes. It remains a remarkable demonstration of Hellenistic technology and astronomical knowledge.

Sponge divers first discovered the wreck in 1900, and salvage operations led by the Greek Navy and archaeologists brought up statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. That lump was later shown to contain gears and inscriptions. Today, the mechanism is held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

The device was enclosed in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its bronze parts, many of them thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. When a crank was turned, it drove a system of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, moving pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

On the front dial, the mechanism showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac along with a calendar. The Moon’s phase appeared by means of a small rotating, partly silvered ball. On the back were two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle, which lasts 19 years and matches solar years to lunar months, and one for the Saros cycle, which lasts about 18 years and was used to predict eclipses. Smaller subsidiary dials tracked additional cycles, including the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

The Moon’s irregular motion, caused by its elliptical orbit, was modeled through a pin-and-slot mechanism that used two gears with offset axes. This reflects the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

Early studies by Valerios Stais, and later by Derek de Solla Price in the 1950s through the 1970s, established the mechanism’s basic function. X-ray imaging in the 1970s, followed by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which began in 2005, used microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging to read much of the inscriptions, which amount to a user’s manual. Researchers have also suggested that the device displayed planetary positions, and reconstructions of that kind of gearing have been published, though the evidence is still incomplete.

The sophistication of the mechanism has no known parallel among surviving artifacts for more than a thousand years, until the appearance of medieval astronomical clocks in Europe and the Islamic world. Its origin is still debated, with possible links to Rhodes, Corinth, or Syracuse, and to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes. It remains a remarkable demonstration of Hellenistic technology and astronomical knowledge.

# Photo Date Renamer

Photo Date Renamer is a simple command-line tool that renames photo files using the date they were taken, pulled from EXIF metadata. The goal is to make photo libraries easier to sort, search, and archive across folders and devices.

## Features

- Renames photos based on the original capture date stored in EXIF metadata
- Supports common image formats, including JPG and JPEG
- Uses consistent, sortable filenames
- Handles duplicate timestamps by adding a counter
- Can process a single folder or scan subfolders recursively
- Includes a dry-run mode so you can preview changes before any files are renamed

## Why use it?

Cameras and phones often create filenames like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`, which stop being useful once those files are mixed into a larger collection. This tool replaces those generic names with timestamp-based filenames like:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

This naming style is easy to read, sorts cleanly, and helps avoid confusion when you combine photos from multiple devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package is published, you may also be able to install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

To rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

To process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

To preview the changes without modifying any files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

To use a custom filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed using this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos have the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix so files are not overwritten.

## Missing metadata

If a file does not have a valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it by default and reports the problem in the summary output. Depending on configuration, future versions may optionally fall back to the file’s creation or modification time.

## Safety

- Never overwrites an existing file without warning
- Supports dry runs for safe previews
- Reports renamed, skipped, and failed files at the end of execution

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you find a bug or want to suggest a feature, please open an issue and include sample filenames, the expected behavior, and your platform details.

## License

MIT License.

A regional airline canceled dozens of flights this week, saying an ongoing shortage of qualified pilots has thrown off schedules and left passengers scrambling for other ways to travel.

The airline, which runs short-haul routes linking smaller cities with major hubs, said the cancellations were needed to maintain safety and meet federal crew-rest and staffing rules. Company officials said they made the call after staffing levels dropped below what was required to operate the full schedule reliably.

“We regret the inconvenience to our customers, but safety remains our top priority,” the airline said in a statement released Tuesday. “Like many regional carriers across the industry, we are facing significant challenges in recruiting and retaining pilots.”

The disruptions hit routes in several states, and some passengers found out only hours before departure that their flights had been removed from the schedule. At several regional airports, travelers reported long lines at customer service desks while airline staff worked to rebook people on later flights or set up ground transportation.

“I was supposed to fly out this morning for a business meeting, and now the next available flight isn’t until tomorrow,” one passenger at a regional airport said. “It’s frustrating because there weren’t many backup options.”

Industry analysts say pilot shortages are becoming a more serious issue for regional airlines, which often act as a training ground for aviators before they move on to larger, better-paying mainline carriers. Regional airlines have had a hard time competing on pay and quality of life, especially as air travel demand has bounced back and larger airlines have stepped up hiring.

The problem has also been made worse by mandatory retirement rules, higher training costs, and stricter experience requirements for new pilots. Taken together, those factors have shrunk the pipeline of available crew members, especially for smaller carriers serving less profitable markets.

Aviation consultant Mark Ellison said regional airlines are often hit the hardest because they have fewer staffing reserves. “When a major airline loses a few pilots, it can sometimes absorb that disruption,” he said. “For a regional carrier, even a small staffing gap can force widespread cancellations.”

The airline said it is offering travel waivers and refunds to affected customers and is working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible. Company officials also said hiring efforts are underway, including recruitment bonuses and expanded training partnerships.

For communities that depend on regional air service, the disruptions highlight a broader concern about how stable air links to smaller markets really are. Local business leaders and airport officials warn that prolonged service cuts could hurt tourism, business travel, and economic activity.

For now, passengers are being advised to check their flight status before heading to the airport, since more schedule changes may still be possible in the coming days.

A fast-moving wildfire near Redwood Canyon National Park forced mandatory evacuations Tuesday as firefighters battled dry conditions, gusty winds, and rugged terrain that officials said were helping drive the blaze.

The fire, called the Canyon Ridge Fire, started late Monday afternoon about five miles east of the park’s southern boundary. By Tuesday evening, it had grown to an estimated 7,800 acres, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Containment remained low as crews worked to protect homes, campgrounds, and critical infrastructure in nearby mountain communities.

Evacuation orders were issued for residents in the small towns of Pine Creek, Alder Grove, and Millstone, along with several rural neighborhoods along Highway 86. Officials also issued an evacuation warning for parts of the park’s gateway communities, where visitors were told to be ready to leave on short notice.

“This fire is moving rapidly and conditions can change minute by minute,” Incident Commander Laura Mendes said during an evening briefing. “Our top priority is life safety — getting people out of harm’s way and giving firefighters the room they need to work.”

As of Tuesday night, no deaths or serious injuries had been reported. Still, officials said several structures were threatened, and at least two outbuildings had been destroyed. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

A stretch of Highway 86 was closed to non-emergency traffic, and park officials temporarily shut down the national park’s southern entrance, along with several backcountry trails and campgrounds. Rangers began escorting campers out of affected areas early Tuesday. Meanwhile, smoke settled into nearby valleys and cut visibility across the region.

The National Weather Service issued a red flag warning for the area, citing low humidity, high temperatures, and wind gusts that could top 30 mph. Fire officials said those conditions were expected to continue into Wednesday, making containment even more difficult.

More than 600 firefighters, backed by air tankers, helicopters, and bulldozers, were assigned to the fire. Crews worked through the night to cut containment lines and protect structures in evacuation zones.

At an evacuation center set up at Redwood County High School, displaced residents arrived with pets, medications, and a few personal belongings. Volunteers handed out food, water, and blankets as families waited for updates.

“We grabbed what we could and left,” said Pine Creek resident Maria Lopez, who evacuated with her husband and two children. “You could see the glow on the ridge, and the wind was just pushing it closer.”

Officials urged residents to keep track of emergency alerts and stay away from the area. “If you have been told to leave, leave now,” Mendes said. “Do not wait to see the fire.”

# Commit Message Style Guide

A good commit message should tell people **what changed** and **why it changed**. That way, someone can understand the project history later without having to read every diff. The goal is to keep commit messages clear, consistent, and concise.

## Structure

Use this format:

```text
<type>: <short summary>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

### 1. Short summary

The summary line should:
- Stay at **50 characters or fewer** when possible
- Use the **imperative mood**: “add”, “fix”, “remove”, not “added” or “fixes”
- Start with a lowercase type followed by a colon
- **Not** end with a period

Examples:
- `fix: handle null response in user service`
- `docs: clarify local setup steps`
- `refactor: simplify cache invalidation logic`

### 2. Body

Add a body when the summary alone doesn’t make the change clear.

A few guidelines:
- Wrap lines at about **72 characters**
- Explain **why** the change was needed before getting into implementation details
- Include context, tradeoffs, side effects, or migration notes when relevant
- Use short paragraphs or bullet points to make it easier to read

A helpful pattern is:
- What problem existed?
- Why was this approach chosen?
- Are there any risks or follow-up tasks?

### 3. Footer

Use footers for metadata when needed, such as:
- Issue references: `Refs: #123`
- Closing references: `Closes: #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: config format has changed`

## Recommended types

It helps to keep the list of types small and predictable. Common options include:
- `feat`: new functionality
- `fix`: bug fix
- `docs`: documentation only
- `refactor`: code change without behavior change
- `test`: tests added or updated
- `chore`: maintenance, tooling, dependency updates
- `perf`: performance improvement
- `build`: build system or dependency management changes
- `ci`: continuous integration changes

## Best practices

- Make each commit represent **one logical change**
- Write the message like a command:
  - “add validation for empty emails”
  - “remove deprecated API client”
- Be specific. For example, prefer:
  - `fix: prevent duplicate invoice creation`
  instead of:
  - `fix: bug fixes`
- If a commit is large or complex, explain it
- Review the message before committing, since it becomes part of the permanent project history

## Avoid

Try not to use:
- Vague summaries like `update stuff` or `misc fixes`
- Overly long subjects
- Messages that describe only the code and not the reason
- Commits that combine unrelated changes
- Auto-generated messages left unedited, such as `WIP` or `temp`

## Example

```text
fix: prevent retry loop on expired auth token

The client kept retrying requests after receiving a 401 response,
which caused unnecessary traffic and delayed user-facing errors.

Stop retries when the token is expired and surface a re-auth
prompt instead.

Closes: #214
```

Consistency matters more than perfection. Having a simple, shared standard makes project history easier to read, search, and maintain.

## Installation

This library works with **Python 3.8+** and is available as a standard Python package.

You can install it with `pip`:

```bash
pip install csvparser
```

If you’re using it inside a project, it’s a good idea to create and activate a virtual environment first:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install csvparser
```

To verify that the installation succeeded:

```bash
python -c "import csvparser; print(csvparser.__version__)"
```

If you want to install from source, clone the repository and install it in editable mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/csvparser.git
cd csvparser
pip install -e .
```

Editable mode is especially helpful during development, because any changes you make to the local code are picked up right away without needing to reinstall the package.

---

## Quick Start

This library is built to make reading and validating CSV data straightforward. In the simplest case, you load a file and loop over the rows as dictionaries.

For example, say you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,30,London
Bob,25,Paris
Charlie,35,Berlin
```

You can parse it like this:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")
rows = parser.read()

for row in rows:
    print(row)
```

Output:

```python
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': '30', 'city': 'London'}
{'name': 'Bob', 'age': '25', 'city': 'Paris'}
{'name': 'Charlie', 'age': '35', 'city': 'Berlin'}
```

### Reading rows one at a time

If you’re working with a large file, it’s better to iterate over the parser instead of loading everything into memory at once:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")

for row in parser:
    print(row["name"], row["city"])
```

### Custom delimiter

If your file uses something other than a comma as the delimiter, you can pass it in when you create the parser:

```python
parser = CSVParser("data.tsv", delimiter="\t")
rows = parser.read()
```

### Header validation

You can also require specific column names:

```python
parser = CSVParser(
    "people.csv",
    required_columns=["name", "age", "city"]
)

rows = parser.read()
```

If any required columns are missing, the parser raises an error early. That makes it easier to catch malformed input before any processing starts.

---

## Error Handling

To handle invalid files gracefully, wrap parsing in a `try`/`except` block:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser, CSVParserError

try:
    rows = CSVParser("people.csv").read()
except CSVParserError as exc:
    print(f"Failed to parse CSV: {exc}")
```

---

## Next Steps

Once you have the basics working, you can build on them by:

- validating row values
- converting string fields to integers, floats, or dates
- skipping empty lines
- integrating parsing into ETL scripts or web backends

For complete API details, check the project documentation or the docstrings in the source code.

**The Fifth Day**

For six years, Sunday evenings filled me with a quiet kind of dread. There was nothing obviously wrong. My job was fine, and the people I worked with were kind. But weekends seemed to disappear almost as soon as they started. Saturday got eaten up by errands and recovery, and Sunday was mostly spent bracing for Monday. It felt like I was living in the leftover edges of my own life.

Then my company launched a pilot program: four days a week, with the same pay and the same expectations for output. I was sure there had to be a catch. I assumed it would mean ten-hour days, or that I’d spend my Fridays off only to come back to a pile of unfinished work.

What happened instead was something I didn’t expect. The work somehow condensed to fit the time available. Meetings that used to drift on for an hour suddenly reached the point in twenty minutes. We stopped setting up meetings just to talk about other meetings. When there are only four workdays, you become protective of them. People got more comfortable saying no, and, strangely enough, all the important things still got done.

The research that followed has matched what I experienced. In the 2022 UK pilot, involving around 61 companies and about 2,900 workers, most firms chose to keep the shorter week afterward. Employees said they were less burned out and sleeping better, and revenue stayed stable. Earlier trials in Iceland found much the same. None of that proves a four-day week would work everywhere, but it does challenge the idea that more hours automatically create more value.

That idea is really the heart of the problem. The five-day week comes from an industrial age, when productivity was tied directly to hours spent on a factory floor. Most of us don’t work like that anymore. Knowledge work depends on attention, and attention doesn’t increase in a straight line. For me, the fifth day was often the one where I was technically at work but mentally absent, replying to emails mostly to show that I was there.

What I got back wasn’t only rest, although the rest mattered. I got ordinary life back. I could go to the dentist without treating it like a logistical puzzle. I could cook an actual dinner on a Friday. I spent a long afternoon with my father, who is older than he used to be, and I realized how much of our relationship had been squeezed into scraps of leftover time. A day off is not really a luxury; it’s room for the parts of life that make someone more than just an employee.

The concerns about fairness are real, and critics are right to raise them. A four-day week is harder to make work for nurses, teachers, and restaurant staff, whose jobs can’t simply be streamlined by cutting meetings. But that seems like an argument for designing it carefully—with staggered shifts, more hiring, and honest measurement—not for dismissing it entirely in places where it could work. And yes, some people will just cram five days into four longer ones, which misses the point. The point isn’t to squeeze the same hours into fewer days. It’s to work fewer hours, and use them better.

I don’t think a four-day week is a cure-all. Bad managers would still be bad managers. Pressure would just find other ways to show up. But after that pilot, I came away with a much clearer sense of what work is supposed to be. It’s part of life, not the thing everything else has to orbit around.

Now, Sunday evenings are quiet. More than any productivity number, that’s what stays with me.

# The Teacher Who Waited

When I was in seventh grade, I had a math teacher named Mr. Okafor who did something that drove me crazy at the time: he wouldn’t just give me the answer.

I was stuck on a word problem about two trains, so I raised my hand, fully expecting the adult in the room to clear things up right away. Mr. Okafor came over, looked at my paper, and asked, “What do you know so far?” I told him I knew nothing. He said, “Great. Let’s write that down.” Then he just waited. Not in an impatient way, not with a sigh, but with the kind of calm that suggested he had all afternoon. Eventually, just to break the silence, I started naming what I did know: the trains left at different times, one of them was faster. And somewhere in the middle of hearing myself say it, I figured it out.

I’ve thought about that moment for years. It showed me something that still feels a little counterintuitive: a good teacher’s job isn’t just to hand over knowledge, but to help build the kind of person who can find it on their own.

Of course, knowing the subject matters. A teacher who doesn’t understand the material can’t help anyone through it. But I’ve known brilliant people who were awful teachers, mostly because they’d forgotten what it feels like not to know something. Expertise can make you impatient with confusion. Mr. Okafor never seemed impatient. He treated confusion like a normal place to be, maybe even an interesting one. And he never made me feel dumb for standing there.

That, I think, is the second quality of a good teacher: they make it safe to be wrong. In his classroom, mistakes ended up on the board for everyone to look at, but not in a shaming way. They were treated like something worth examining. “Interesting,” he’d say. “Where did this go sideways?” We learned to track down our own mistakes like detectives instead of hiding them like evidence. I’ve carried that with me into adulthood, where admitting an error early is often what separates a small problem from a disaster.

The third quality is harder to pin down. Good teachers believe in you a little before you’ve earned it. One time, Mr. Okafor gave me a problem from a competition packet meant for older students and said, “I think you’d enjoy this one.” I never solved it. But I spent a week trying, and I still remember what it felt like to be taken seriously. His confidence in me felt like a loan, and I wanted to work hard enough to pay it back.

Since then, I’ve had teachers who were more charismatic, more entertaining, more well-known. Some of them were wonderful. But when I think about the people who actually changed the way I think, I come back to the man who stood next to my desk and let the silence sit there until I filled it myself.

Teaching that way takes a certain kind of restraint. It would have been much quicker for him to show me the solution, and I probably would have appreciated that for about ten minutes. Instead, he gave me something slower but far more lasting: the experience of working it out for myself, and the quiet realization that I could.

I don’t remember the answer to the train problem. What I remember is the waiting. I think that’s the whole point.

Skyline Air said Monday that it will cancel about 120 flights over the next six weeks because it does not have enough qualified pilots, a shortage the company says has become critical.

The cuts will hit service to eight mid-sized and rural markets, including Cedar Falls, Marlow County, and Pine Harbor. According to the airline, three of those communities will lose daily service altogether until at least mid-March.

“We deeply regret the disruption to our customers and the communities we serve,” said Dana Whitfield, Skyline Air’s chief operating officer. “We have exhausted every option to cover these routes safely and within federal duty-time regulations. Without enough pilots, we cannot operate the schedule we promised.”

Skyline said it has lost nearly 15 percent of its pilot workforce over the past year as many pilots left for major airlines that offer higher pay, signing bonuses, and quicker paths to international routes. The airline now employs about 340 pilots, down from 400 last January.

Analysts say Skyline’s situation is part of a broader national problem. A wave of retirements among experienced pilots, along with a federal rule requiring airline captains to log 1,500 flight hours, has squeezed the pipeline of new hires. Regional carriers, which often act as stepping stones to the major airlines, have been especially hard hit.

“Regionals are the farm system of the industry,” said aviation consultant Marcus Tran. “When the big airlines hire aggressively, the regionals bleed talent. Then the small towns that depend on them lose air service, and it’s very hard to get it back.”

Travelers are already feeling the effects. At Cedar Falls Regional Airport on Monday, Priya Natarajan said her flight to a family wedding was canceled with just two days’ notice. “I got a text and an email, and that was it,” she said. “Now I’m looking at a five-hour drive to the nearest hub.”

Local leaders say the consequences could last longer than the immediate disruption. Cedar Falls Mayor Tom Hendricks said dependable air service is important for attracting employers and helping local businesses. “Losing flights isn’t just an inconvenience,” he said. “It affects our economy.”

Skyline said passengers affected by the cancellations will get full refunds or, when possible, be rebooked on partner airlines. The carrier also announced a new retention package that includes raises of up to 18 percent and a tuition-assistance program for aspiring pilots.

Whitfield said Skyline hopes to restore full service by April but would not guarantee a timeline.
