## Public Bike-Share Service FAQ

### 1. What is the bike-share service?
Our bike-share service is a convenient, affordable, and eco-friendly way to get around the city. You can unlock a bike at one station, ride to where you’re going, and return it to any available station in the network.

### 2. How do I sign up?
You can sign up on our website or through our mobile app. Just create an account, choose a pass or membership, and add a payment method. Once you’re registered, you can unlock bikes directly from the app.

### 3. What types of passes are available?
We offer a few different options to suit different needs, including single rides, day passes, and monthly or annual memberships. Short-term passes work well for visitors, while memberships are a better fit for regular riders. You can find current pricing on our website and in the app.

### 4. How do I unlock a bike?
Open the app, find a nearby station or available bike, and either scan the QR code or enter the bike number. The lock will release automatically. If you run into any issues, customer support is available to help.

### 5. Where can I return a bike?
You should return bikes to any official bike-share station that has an open dock. Make sure the bike is securely locked in place, and wait for confirmation in the app so you don’t get charged extra.

### 6. Is there a time limit for rides?
Yes. Ride time limits vary depending on the pass or membership you have. If you go over the included ride period, extra fees may apply. You can check your ride details anytime in the app.

### 7. What if a station is full?
If the station you’re heading to is full, the app will show you nearby stations with open docks. In some cases, you may qualify for a grace period so you can return the bike at the next closest station.

### 8. What should I do if a bike is damaged?
If you notice a problem before or during your ride, report it in the app right away and choose another bike if necessary. This helps us keep the fleet safe and in good condition.

### 9. Do I need to wear a helmet?
We strongly recommend that all riders wear a helmet, and local law may require it for certain age groups. Please check local regulations before you ride.

### 10. What happens if a bike is lost or stolen?
If your bike is lost or stolen during your rental, contact customer support immediately and file a police report if required. Charges may apply until the bike is recovered or the case is resolved.

### 11. How can I contact customer support?
You can reach customer support through the app, the website, or by phone. Check our Help section for current contact details and service hours.

I grew up in a family where meat was just part of life, as ordinary and unquestioned as the furniture in the house. We had roast chicken on Sundays, bacon on weekends, and burgers in the summer. No one talked about whether eating animals was right or wrong, because it never seemed like there was a moral issue to discuss. Meat was simply food, and food was what kept the family fed and brought everyone together at the table. If gratitude was expressed, it went to the person who cooked the meal, not to the animal that had died for it.

My thinking about that didn’t change because of one dramatic moment. It changed gradually, through a series of small discomforts that kept building. I remember standing in a grocery store, looking at packaged cuts of meat, and feeling for maybe the first time how strange the gap was between what I was seeing and the living being it had once been. The neat plastic wrapping seemed meant not just to preserve the meat, but to shield me from thinking too hard about where it came from. And once I started thinking about it, I couldn’t really stop. I began to see that my appetite relied on a kind of selective attention: I liked animals in the abstract, but when they were on my plate, I preferred not to picture them at all.

As I understand it now, the ethical problem of eating meat starts with that avoidance. Most people would probably agree that animal suffering matters, at least to some degree. We can recognize pain in a dog, fear in a cow, agitation in a chicken. And yet the food system often treats these animals less like living creatures with their own experiences and more like production units. If causing unnecessary suffering is wrong, then industrial meat production is especially difficult to justify. The scale of confinement, mutilation, and slaughter is so enormous that it almost becomes hard to grasp, and maybe that is part of why it continues. It is easier to take part in cruelty when that cruelty is hidden behind branding, habit, and convenience.

At the same time, I don’t want to flatten this into a simple display of moral purity. Eating meat is entangled with culture, class, geography, and memory. For some people it is about tradition; for others it is connected to survival, health, or a lack of access to alternatives. I don’t think ethics is helped by acting as though everyone is making choices from the same set of options. Someone buying cheap meat while trying to feed a family on a tight budget is not in the same position as someone treating animal products as a luxury. Moral judgment without any social context can easily turn into self-congratulation.

Even so, complexity shouldn’t become a way of excusing indifference. The fact that nobody can live perfectly does not mean nobody has to try. I haven’t arrived at a pure or final answer. I eat less meat than I used to, and when I do eat it, I feel the weight of that decision more consciously. For me, the ethics of eating meat is not just about whether killing animals can ever be justified. It is also about whether I am willing to let comfort keep me from paying attention. If it is possible to eat ethically, then maybe it starts with refusing that silence—by looking honestly at what nourishes us, what it costs, and who ends up paying the price.

The Smaller Person

When I was thirty-four, I stood in a bakery in Lisbon quietly rehearsing a sentence in my head. All I wanted was a coffee and a custard tart. I’d practiced what to say on the way there, but the moment the woman behind the counter looked at me, the words vanished. In the end, I just pointed and said “this” twice. She gave me a kind smile, the kind you’d give a child, and I felt my face flush.

That was the first thing Portuguese taught me: how much of my identity as an adult depended on sounding capable. Back home, I was the kind of person people came to for answers. In that bakery, I had the vocabulary of a toddler and the pride of a department head, and those two things did not mix well.

For months, I felt like a reduced version of myself. I couldn’t joke properly, make an argument, or toss out the kind of casual observation that makes someone seem vivid and distinct. I’d always thought my personality was something stable, but it turned out to rely a lot more on grammar than I realized. What remained was a simpler version of me: patient, slightly earnest, frequently confused. Oddly enough, people seemed to like that person. My neighbor, Dona Fernanda, who was seventy and had never been outside Portugal, took it upon herself to correct my Portuguese with great seriousness. “Not *eu sou cansado*,” she’d say. “*Estou* cansado. You are tired, but you are not made of tired.” I never forgot that distinction between permanent and temporary states, and I still think about it even in English.

The second thing I learned was how to listen. In my first language, I listened carelessly, often while already planning what I was going to say next. In Portuguese, I had to pay attention to every word as if it were being tossed to me and I had to catch it. I started noticing people’s tone, their gestures, the pauses they left between thoughts. It made me a better listener in both languages, and I was a little embarrassed to realize how much I’d missed before.

The third lesson was that mistakes don’t destroy you. Once, at a dinner table, I announced that I was “very constipated” when what I meant was embarrassed. They’re false friends, and I’ll leave it at that. Everyone burst out laughing, someone topped off my glass, and I felt more included in that moment than I had all week. What I learned was that failing in public usually makes people warmer toward you, not colder. I’d spent years trying to avoid exactly the kind of experience that might have made me loosen up.

For a long time, my progress felt invisible. I thought I was stuck. Then one afternoon, I realized I had followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed exactly when I was supposed to. No one handed me a certificate. There was no announcement. A door I hadn’t even realized was closed was suddenly open.

I still make mistakes every day, and I still notice the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. But I don’t hear it as pity anymore. I hear it as hospitality, something offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

What I took from those years wasn’t exactly fluency. It was a willingness to be the smaller person, to point at something and say “this,” and then try again. That person, it turns out, was never lesser. He was just learning, and learning was the very thing I had stopped allowing myself to do.

For months, I felt like a reduced version of myself. I couldn’t joke properly, make an argument, or toss out the kind of casual observation that makes someone seem vivid and distinct. I’d always thought my personality was something stable, but it turned out to rely a lot more on grammar than I realized. What remained was a simpler version of me: patient, slightly earnest, frequently confused. Oddly enough, people seemed to like that person. My neighbor, Dona Fernanda, who was seventy and had never been outside Portugal, took it upon herself to correct my Portuguese with great seriousness. “Not *eu sou cansado*,” she’d say. “*Estou* cansado. You are tired, but you are not made of tired.” I never forgot that distinction between permanent and temporary states, and I still think about it even in English.

The second thing I learned was how to listen. In my first language, I listened carelessly, often while already planning what I was going to say next. In Portuguese, I had to pay attention to every word as if it were being tossed to me and I had to catch it. I started noticing people’s tone, their gestures, the pauses they left between thoughts. It made me a better listener in both languages, and I was a little embarrassed to realize how much I’d missed before.

The third lesson was that mistakes don’t destroy you. Once, at a dinner table, I announced that I was “very constipated” when what I meant was embarrassed. They’re false friends, and I’ll leave it at that. Everyone burst out laughing, someone topped off my glass, and I felt more included in that moment than I had all week. What I learned was that failing in public usually makes people warmer toward you, not colder. I’d spent years trying to avoid exactly the kind of experience that might have made me loosen up.

For a long time, my progress felt invisible. I thought I was stuck. Then one afternoon, I realized I had followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed exactly when I was supposed to. No one handed me a certificate. There was no announcement. A door I hadn’t even realized was closed was suddenly open.

I still make mistakes every day, and I still notice the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. But I don’t hear it as pity anymore. I hear it as hospitality, something offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

What I took from those years wasn’t exactly fluency. It was a willingness to be the smaller person, to point at something and say “this,” and then try again. That person, it turns out, was never lesser. He was just learning, and learning was the very thing I had stopped allowing myself to do.

The **Erie Canal** is a historic canal in New York State that runs from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Finished in 1825, it was the first navigable waterway to connect the Atlantic coast with the Great Lakes, and it played a major role in the economic development of the United States during the nineteenth century.

## History

Ideas for a canal across upstate New York had been circulating since the late eighteenth century, but the project really moved forward because of Governor DeWitt Clinton. After federal support failed to appear, he secured state funding in 1817. Detractors mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began on July 4, 1817, in Rome, New York.

The canal was built mostly by hand by laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, using horses, oxen, and simple tools. Engineers such as Benjamin Wright and James Geddes had little formal training and learned as they went, developing ways to clear forests, remove stumps, and work through swampland. The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep, with 83 locks to manage an elevation change of about 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial trip and, in what became known as the "Wedding of the Waters," poured water from Lake Erie into the Atlantic Ocean.

## Economic and social impact

The canal sharply cut both the cost and time required to move freight. The cost of shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City dropped from about $100 to around $10, and travel times fell from weeks to just days. Farm products from the Midwest moved east, while manufactured goods and settlers headed west.

New York City overtook competing ports like Philadelphia and Boston and became the country’s leading commercial center. Cities along the canal route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, expanded quickly. The region also became a center of social change, with ties to religious revivalism, the women’s rights movement, and abolitionism. Because of this, some historians have called western New York the "burned-over district."

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged from 1836 to 1862. Later, between 1905 and 1918, it was replaced by the larger **New York State Barge Canal**, which used rivers and lakes as part of its route. In the twentieth century, railroads, highways, and the St. Lawrence Seaway reduced canal commerce.

Today, the canal is used mainly for recreation, including boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress created the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to help preserve its legacy. The canal is still operated by the New York State Canal Corporation.

## See also

- DeWitt Clinton
- Great Lakes
- Hudson River
- Transportation in New York

I used to see cars as a symbol of freedom. When I was younger, it felt like a city really began where the traffic got heavier—the bright lights, the constant movement, the low hum of engines idling at red lights. A crowded street seemed to signal that a place mattered. If everyone was trying to get there, then that had to be where life was happening. But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve started noticing more of what traffic takes away. I notice how sirens interrupt conversations, how exhaust lingers in the air on hot summer afternoons, and how people are pushed to the edges of narrow sidewalks while long lines of cars sit motionless in the middle of the street. So when I think about whether cars should be banned from city centers, I find myself leaning toward yes—not because I hate cars, but because I think the center of a city should belong to people first.

What changed my mind wasn’t a statistic, even though there are plenty of convincing ones about pollution and safety. It was more of a feeling. In the few places I’ve been where cars were restricted or not allowed at all, I felt an almost instant sense of relief. People walked down the middle of the street without worrying. Children moved the way children do—unpredictably—and no one seemed irritated by it. Outdoor tables felt like places to stay awhile, not tiny islands surrounded by noise. Without cars, the city didn’t feel empty. It felt more fully inhabited by people.

A city center, after all, is more than just a route from one place to another. It’s where a city shows itself to itself. It’s where tourists get their first impression, where office workers step out for lunch, where older people try to cross the street, where protests come together, and where strangers become part of the same crowd. If that space is mainly shaped around vehicles, then that says something troubling about what we value. It means we’ve chosen speed over connection, convenience over community.

Of course, banning cars from city centers isn’t as easy as covering over a road. There are obvious objections, and some of them are important. Disabled people, delivery drivers, emergency services, and people commuting from places with weak public transportation can’t just be ignored. Small businesses may worry about losing customers. Any policy that pretends these problems don’t exist will feel less like progress and more like punishment.

That’s why I don’t think a ban should be absolute or careless. It should be designed thoughtfully, with exemptions, dependable public transit, better cycling infrastructure, and clear plans for deliveries and accessibility. The point isn’t to attack drivers. It’s to ask what kind of city life we actually want to create.

Cars are useful, but city centers are too important to be built around them. If we take cars out of those spaces—carefully, fairly, and with real alternatives in place—we may find that what looked like a sacrifice is actually a kind of recovery. We may regain cleaner air, quieter streets, and a stronger sense that the heart of a city is not its traffic, but its people.

I still remember what it felt like to walk into my local public library when I was a kid and immediately know I was somewhere different. It was quiet, but never cold or overly formal. It felt full, not only of books, but of possibility. I didn’t have the language then to explain what the library meant to me, but I understood it on instinct: it was a place where I was welcome without having to buy anything, prove anything, or be any particular kind of person. I’ve carried that feeling with me ever since, and it’s one of the reasons I believe public libraries still matter so much.

At a time when almost any piece of information seems to be available on a phone in seconds, it’s easy to think of libraries as nice but outdated. If you can order books online and search for articles instantly, what role is left for the library? To me, the answer is straightforward: a public library does far more than store information. It makes knowledge accessible, dignity available, and community visible.

What matters most about a public library is that it’s one of the few genuinely public spaces we still have. So many places in modern life come with the expectation that you’ll spend money if you want to remain there. Cafés, stores, and entertainment venues all carry an unspoken price of admission. A library asks for nothing except respect for the shared space. You can sit, read, think, learn, or simply rest. That kind of openness is unusual, and it says something hopeful about what a community believes people deserve.

Libraries also matter because access to information is not nearly as equal as we often like to imagine. Not everyone has dependable internet, a quiet place at home, up-to-date technology, or the money to buy books and subscriptions. For many people, the public library helps close those gaps. It provides computers, internet access, job resources, research support, language learning, and educational programs. For a student, it can be a place to study. For someone looking for work, it can be where a résumé gets written and submitted. For an immigrant, it can be a bridge into a new community. For someone who is lonely, it can simply be a place to feel less alone.

I also believe libraries matter because they make room for a slower, more thoughtful kind of discovery. Online, we’re often directed by algorithms that serve us more of what they think we already like. In a library, we can wander. We can take a book off the shelf because the title catches us off guard or because it happens to be next to the one we came for. That kind of unexpected encounter can widen a life. Libraries remind us that learning isn’t only about efficiency; it’s also about curiosity.

More than anything, public libraries still matter because they express a democratic ideal: that knowledge should not belong only to the people who can afford it. A library is a quiet argument against exclusion. It says that stories, facts, history, imagination, and opportunity are meant to be shared.

That’s why libraries still feel essential to me. They aren’t relics from an earlier era. They are living promises. In their own modest way, they remind us that a community is strongest when it invests in places where everyone is free to enter and grow.

Create a new event on a specific calendar by sending a `POST` request to:

```http
POST /v1/calendars/{calendar_id}/events
```

You’ll need to authenticate with a Bearer token that includes the `calendar.events.write` scope.

The path parameter `calendar_id` is the ID of the calendar you want to use. If you want the user’s default calendar, use `primary`.

In the request body, include:
- `title` (string, required): the event title, up to 200 characters.
- `start` (string, required): the start time in ISO 8601 format, for example `2025-07-01T14:00:00Z`.
- `end` (string, required): the end time, which must be after `start`.
- `timezone` (string, optional): an IANA time zone such as `America/New_York`. If you don’t provide one, the calendar’s time zone is used.
- `description` (string, optional): event details, up to 5,000 characters.
- `location` (string, optional): a physical address or meeting URL.
- `attendees` (array, optional): a list of objects that each include an `email` field and can also include an optional `optional` boolean.
- `reminders` (array, optional): a list of objects with a `method` of either `email` or `popup`, plus `minutes_before`.
- `recurrence` (string, optional): an RRULE string such as `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=10`.
- `send_notifications` (boolean, optional): whether invitation emails should be sent. This defaults to `true`.

Example request:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/calendars/primary/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Project Kickoff",
    "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
    "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
    "location": "https://meet.example.com/kickoff",
    "attendees": [
      { "email": "jordan@example.com" },
      { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true }
    ],
    "reminders": [{ "method": "popup", "minutes_before": 10 }]
  }'
```

If the event is created successfully, the API returns `201 Created` and a response like this:

```json
{
  "id": "evt_8f3k29x",
  "calendar_id": "primary",
  "title": "Project Kickoff",
  "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
  "status": "confirmed",
  "attendees": [
    { "email": "jordan@example.com", "response": "pending" },
    { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true, "response": "pending" }
  ],
  "created_at": "2025-06-20T09:12:44Z",
  "url": "https://calendar.example.com/events/evt_8f3k29x"
}
```

Possible errors include:
- `400 invalid_request`: a required field is missing, a date is malformed, or `end` is before `start`.
- `401 unauthorized`: the token is missing, invalid, or expired.
- `403 insufficient_scope`: the token does not have write permission for this calendar.
- `404 calendar_not_found`: the specified calendar doesn’t exist.
- `409 conflict`: an identical event already exists when you use an idempotency key.
- `429 rate_limited`: too many requests were made. Retry after the amount of time in the `Retry-After` header.

A few important notes:
- For idempotency, include an `Idempotency-Key` header so you can safely retry a request without creating duplicates.
- The rate limit is 60 requests per minute per user.
- You can include up to 200 attendees per event.
- For all-day events, send date-only values such as `2025-07-01` for `start` and `end`. The `end` date is exclusive.

Friendship used to feel smaller to me, but it also felt more personal. When I was younger, a friend was someone I saw at school, someone whose house I’d been to, someone whose voice I could recognize without looking at a screen. If I wanted to tell them something, I had to wait until lunch or call their house and hope their parents didn’t pick up. There was a slowness to that kind of friendship, and sometimes it was frustrating, but it also gave things a certain weight. Every interaction felt intentional. You had to make the time.

Social media changed all of that. At first, it felt incredible, almost like a miracle. All of a sudden, friendship wasn’t limited by distance, schedules, or even shyness. I could stay in touch with people from old schools, summer programs, family trips, and eventually from different parts of my life. Someone I hadn’t seen in years could still show up in my day through a photo, a joke, a birthday post, or a message sent after midnight. Social media made friendship feel ongoing, like no one ever had to completely vanish.

There’s something genuinely beautiful about that. I’ve been able to see the ordinary details of my friends’ lives in ways that would have been impossible before: their new apartments, bad haircuts, pets, travel pictures, engagements, breakups, and small private victories. I’ve gotten to celebrate people I otherwise might have lost touch with. Sometimes even a quick reaction to a story can open a door again. A friendship that might have faded can keep going through tiny digital gestures. Social media has made it easier to say, “I’m still here. I still know you.”

At the same time, it has changed friendship in ways that can feel unsettling. It creates a sense of intimacy without always asking for the effort that real intimacy takes. I can know what someone ate, where they went on vacation, and what political opinion they posted, while still having no real idea how they’re actually doing. I can feel caught up on someone’s life without ever asking a sincere question. In that way, social media can turn friendship into passive observation. We watch each other instead of really meeting.

It has also blurred what the word “friend” even means. The number can climb into the hundreds or even thousands, but that kind of abundance can sometimes cover up a different kind of loneliness. Being visible is not the same thing as being known. Getting likes is not the same thing as being comforted. Social media encourages performance, and friendship can get tangled up in presentation. Instead of simply sharing ourselves, we can start curating ourselves, even for people who genuinely care about us. The pressure to seem happy, funny, successful, or unaffected can make honesty feel dangerous.

Still, I don’t think social media has ruined friendship. I think it has exposed both what friendship does well and where it falls short. It can help us stay connected, but it can’t replace real presence. It can start conversations, but it can’t promise depth. The friendships that matter most in my life are the ones that exist both online and offline: the people I can send memes to, but also call when I’m in crisis; the people who notice when I go quiet; the people who know the version of me that exists beyond a profile.

Social media changed friendship by making it broader, faster, and more constant. But it also taught me that real friendship is still built the old-fashioned way: through attention, honesty, time, and care.

Social media made friendship feel ongoing, like no one ever had to completely vanish.

There’s something genuinely beautiful about that. I’ve been able to see the ordinary details of my friends’ lives in ways that would have been impossible before: their new apartments, bad haircuts, pets, travel pictures, engagements, breakups, and small private victories. I’ve gotten to celebrate people I otherwise might have lost touch with. Sometimes even a quick reaction to a story can open a door again. A friendship that might have faded can keep going through tiny digital gestures. Social media has made it easier to say, “I’m still here. I still know you.”

At the same time, it has changed friendship in ways that can feel unsettling. It creates a sense of intimacy without always asking for the effort that real intimacy takes. I can know what someone ate, where they went on vacation, and what political opinion they posted, while still having no real idea how they’re actually doing. I can feel caught up on someone’s life without ever asking a sincere question. In that way, social media can turn friendship into passive observation. We watch each other instead of really meeting.

It has also blurred what the word “friend” even means. The number can climb into the hundreds or even thousands, but that kind of abundance can sometimes cover up a different kind of loneliness. Being visible is not the same thing as being known. Getting likes is not the same thing as being comforted. Social media encourages performance, and friendship can get tangled up in presentation. Instead of simply sharing ourselves, we can start curating ourselves, even for people who genuinely care about us. The pressure to seem happy, funny, successful, or unaffected can make honesty feel dangerous.

Still, I don’t think social media has ruined friendship. I think it has exposed both what friendship does well and where it falls short. It can help us stay connected, but it can’t replace real presence. It can start conversations, but it can’t promise depth. The friendships that matter most in my life are the ones that exist both online and offline: the people I can send memes to, but also call when I’m in crisis; the people who notice when I go quiet; the people who know the version of me that exists beyond a profile.

Social media changed friendship by making it broader, faster, and more constant. But it also taught me that real friendship is still built the old-fashioned way: through attention, honesty, time, and care.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia, set along the banks of the Mtkvari River in the eastern part of the country. With a population of over one million, it serves as Georgia’s political, economic, and cultural center. Because of its location at the meeting point of Europe and Asia, Tbilisi has long been an important center for trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange.

The city’s name comes from the Georgian word “tbili,” meaning “warm,” referring to the natural sulfur hot springs found there. Tradition says that Tbilisi was founded in the 5th century by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia, who discovered the springs while hunting. Archaeological evidence, though, shows that the area was settled even earlier. Tbilisi later became the capital of the eastern Georgian kingdom and grew into a major urban center along regional trade routes.

Over the centuries, Tbilisi was often fought over by major regional powers, including the Persians, Arabs, Byzantines, Seljuks, Mongols, and Ottomans. In the 19th century, it also came under the influence of Russian imperial expansion and became an important administrative center of the Russian Empire in the Caucasus. After periods of brief independence and Soviet rule, Tbilisi became the capital of independent Georgia in 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Tbilisi is especially known for its varied architecture, which shows the many layers of its history. The Old Town has narrow streets, traditional wooden balconies, churches, mosques, and bathhouses, while newer parts of the city include neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet modernist, and contemporary architecture. Among its best-known landmarks are Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sameba Cathedral, Rustaveli Avenue, and the historic sulfur baths of Abanotubani.

The city is also one of Georgia’s main centers for education, the arts, and science. It is home to Tbilisi State University, one of the oldest universities in the Caucasus, along with museums, theaters, galleries, and research institutions. Leading cultural institutions include the Georgian National Museum, the Shota Rustaveli Theatre, and the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre.

Tbilisi has a diverse economy built on services, finance, tourism, transportation, and industry. It is also the country’s main transportation hub, with an international airport, railway links, and a metro system. In recent decades, the city has seen extensive redevelopment and modernization, while still preserving much of its historic character.

Today, Tbilisi is known for its multicultural heritage, lively public life, and distinctive urban landscape. It remains one of the most important cities in the South Caucasus and a powerful symbol of Georgian statehood and identity.

# Library of Alexandria

The **Library of Alexandria**, located in Alexandria, Egypt, was one of the largest and most renowned libraries of the ancient world. Founded in the early 3rd century BCE during the Ptolemaic dynasty, it was part of a larger research institution called the Mouseion (Museum), which was dedicated to the Muses. Over time, the library came to symbolize both ancient scholarship and, in popular culture, the tragic loss of knowledge through destruction.

## History

The library was most likely established either during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (r. 305–282 BCE) or that of his son, Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 284–246 BCE). An Athenian exile, Demetrius of Phalerum, is traditionally said to have helped plan its creation, although modern scholars question how much involvement he actually had. The Ptolemaic rulers aimed to collect texts from across the known world. Ancient accounts say that ships arriving in Alexandria's harbor were searched for books, which were then copied and, in some cases, retained, while the original owners were given the copies.

## Collection and scholarship

Estimates of the library’s size differ dramatically, with ancient writers giving numbers ranging from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, though these figures are generally seen as unreliable. The collection covered literature, history, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy. Most of the works were in Greek, though some were translations from other languages. Tradition also holds that the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there, resulting in the Septuagint.

The library drew many notable scholars. Euclid is linked with Alexandria and is said to have produced his *Elements* there. Eratosthenes, who served as librarian, calculated the circumference of the Earth. Other important figures included Aristarchus of Samothrace, who edited Homeric texts, and Callimachus, who created the *Pinakes*, an early catalog of the library’s holdings. In the city as well, Herophilus and Erasistratus made important advances in the study of anatomy.

## Decline and destruction

The library did not disappear in a single event; its decline appears to have been gradual. In 48 BCE, a fire set by Julius Caesar during his conflict in Alexandria damaged part of the city and may have destroyed some books, although the scale of the damage is uncertain. Under Roman rule, the library lost funding and royal support. In the 270s CE, Aurelian’s campaign devastated the district that contained the Mouseion. In 391 CE, the Serapeum, often described as a "daughter library," was destroyed under Bishop Theophilus. The later story that the Arab conqueror Amr ibn al-As burned the library in 642 CE is considered by most historians to be a legend that emerged afterward.

## Modern legacy

In 2002, Egypt opened the **Bibliotheca Alexandrina** near the site of the ancient library. It serves as a modern library and cultural center meant to revive the spirit of the original institution.

## See also

- Ptolemaic Kingdom
- Library of Pergamum
- Septuagint

# Plugin System Documentation

## Overview

The editor’s plugin system makes it possible to add new functionality without changing the core application. Plugins are written in JavaScript and run inside an isolated sandbox, where they communicate with the editor through a controlled API.

## Installing Plugins

To install a plugin manually, place its folder in your user plugin directory:

- **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\Editor\plugins`
- **macOS/Linux:** `~/.config/editor/plugins`

You can also open the command palette with `Ctrl+Shift+P` and run **Plugins: Install from Registry**. To activate newly installed plugins, restart the editor or run **Plugins: Reload All**.

## Plugin Structure

Every plugin needs its own folder with at least these two files:

```text
my-plugin/
├── manifest.json
└── index.js
```

### manifest.json

The manifest defines the plugin:

```json
{
  "name": "word-counter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "permissions": ["editor.read", "ui.statusbar"],
  "activationEvents": ["onStartup"]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `name` | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `version` | Semantic version string |
| `main` | Entry point file |
| `permissions` | APIs the plugin may access |
| `activationEvents` | When the plugin loads |

## Writing a Plugin

The entry file must export an `activate` function. If the plugin needs to clean up resources, it should also export `deactivate`.

```javascript
exports.activate = function (editor) {
  const item = editor.ui.createStatusItem();

  editor.on("textChanged", () => {
    const text = editor.document.getText();
    item.setText(`Words: ${text.split(/\s+/).length}`);
  });
};

exports.deactivate = function () {
  // Release resources here
};
```

## Core API

- **`editor.document`**: Read and modify the active file with methods like `getText()`, `insert()`, and `replace()`
- **`editor.commands`**: Register commands using `registerCommand(id, handler)`
- **`editor.ui`**: Create status items, menus, and panels
- **`editor.on(event, callback)`**: Subscribe to events like `textChanged`, `fileSaved`, and `selectionChanged`
- **`editor.settings`**: Read user configuration values

## Permissions

A plugin can only use the APIs listed in its manifest. Common permissions include:

- `editor.read`: Read document contents
- `editor.write`: Modify documents
- `ui.statusbar`: Add status bar items
- `fs.read`: Read files in the workspace
- `network`: Make external requests

When a plugin is installed for the first time, users are prompted to approve its permissions.

## Debugging

To view output from `console.log` and any uncaught errors, open **Help → Toggle Plugin Console**. After making changes, use **Plugins: Reload All** to see updates right away.

## Best Practices

1. Request only the permissions you actually need.
2. Prefer specific activation events over `onStartup` to keep launch times fast.
3. Clean up event listeners in `deactivate`.
4. Avoid blocking operations; use asynchronous calls for file and network access.

# Design Document: API Caching Layer

## Overview

This document recommends adding a distributed caching layer to our web API to reduce load on the database, improve response times, and help the system scale better during peak traffic.

## Problem Statement

Right now, every API request goes straight to the primary PostgreSQL database. Profiling shows that 80% of our traffic is hitting read-only endpoints like product catalogs, user profiles, and configuration data, and many of those requests return the same results over and over. During peak hours, p95 latency goes above 800ms, and database CPU usage regularly hits 85%.

## Goals

- Bring p95 latency on read endpoints down to under 150ms
- Reduce database read load by at least 60%
- Keep data freshness within acceptable limits, with staleness under 60 seconds for most resources
- Make these improvements without changing any client-facing API contracts

## Non-Goals

- Caching authenticated write operations
- Replacing the database as the source of truth

## Proposed Solution

We should introduce **Redis** as a cache-aside layer between the API servers and the database.

On the **read path**, the API would first check Redis using a deterministic key such as `product:v1:{id}`. If the value is in cache, the API returns it immediately. If not, it queries the database, stores the result in Redis with a TTL, and then returns it.

On the **write path**, when data is updated or deleted, the API would invalidate the relevant cache keys. For list and search results, we would use short TTLs of 30 seconds instead of explicit invalidation, since tracking all of those dependencies tends to be error-prone.

For **key design**:
- Version prefixes would let us do bulk invalidation after schema changes
- Per-user data would include the user ID in the key so data cannot leak between users

For the **TTL strategy**:

| Resource | TTL |
|---|---|
| Configuration | 10 min |
| Product details | 5 min (plus invalidation) |
| Lists/search | 30 sec |

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Stampedes:** If popular keys expire at the same time, a large number of requests could hit the database at once. To reduce that risk, we’ll use request coalescing and add random jitter of ±10% to TTLs.
- **Stale data:** Explicit invalidation on writes, combined with conservative TTLs, should keep stale data exposure limited.
- **Redis outage:** If Redis goes down, the API will fall back to the database behind a circuit breaker. That means performance may degrade, but requests should still succeed instead of failing outright.
- **Memory growth:** We’ll enforce `allkeys-lru` eviction and monitor memory usage closely.

## Rollout Plan

1. Deploy a managed Redis cluster with replication
2. Implement caching behind a feature flag, starting with configuration endpoints
3. Roll out by endpoint in stages: 10%, then 50%, then 100% of traffic
4. Monitor hit rate, latency, and error rates at each stage

## Success Metrics

We’ll consider this successful if cache hit rate stays above 75%, p95 latency is under 150ms, and database CPU stays below 50% during peak traffic.

## Open Questions

- Should we add an in-process L1 cache for extremely hot keys?
- Is a CDN a good fit for public, unauthenticated endpoints?

Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe that launched on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program to explore the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It was launched sixteen days after its twin, Voyager 2, and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth, moving at about 17 kilometers per second, or roughly 61,000 km/h, relative to the Sun.

The Voyager program was designed around a rare alignment of the outer planets that happens about once every 175 years. That alignment made it possible for spacecraft to use gravity assists to travel from one planet to another. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory built the probes, which were originally funded for a four-year mission focused on Jupiter and Saturn.

At launch, Voyager 1 had a mass of about 825 kilograms. It uses a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna to communicate with the Deep Space Network. Its power comes from three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs, which turn heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Because their power output drops by several watts each year, engineers have had to gradually shut down nonessential instruments and heaters. The spacecraft also carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated phonograph record filled with sounds, images, and music meant to represent life and culture on Earth.

Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter on March 5, 1979. During that encounter, it discovered active volcanism on Io, the first volcanic activity ever observed beyond Earth. It reached Saturn on November 12, 1980, and sent back detailed images of the rings as well as Saturn’s largest moon, Titan, whose thick atmosphere it studied closely. The flyby of Titan changed the spacecraft’s path, bending it out of the ecliptic plane and bringing its planetary tour to an end. In 1990, Voyager 1 took the “Family Portrait” of the Solar System, which included the famous image of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot.

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium, becoming the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument detected a sharp increase in plasma density, which confirmed that crossing.

In November 2023, the probe started sending unintelligible data because of a fault in one of its onboard computers. Engineers at JPL traced the problem to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem. In 2024, they restored communication by relocating the affected code, a remarkable achievement considering the spacecraft was more than 24 billion kilometers away.

Voyager 1 is still transmitting data about magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect its RTGs to keep at least one instrument running into the mid-2020s, and possibly longer. Built with technology from around 1977, the probe will continue drifting silently through the Milky Way and is expected to pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in roughly 40,000 years.

See also: Voyager 2, Voyager program, Pioneer 10, Golden Record

# The Last Free Room

When I was nine, my family moved to a new town in the dead of winter, and for weeks I didn’t know a single person. My mother was working two jobs. My father was still in our old city, finishing out a lease. The apartment was small, quiet, and the afternoons felt endless. Then one day, I followed a stranger’s dog down the street and wound up standing in front of the public library.

I didn’t realize it at the time, but I’d stumbled onto the one place in town that wanted nothing from me.

That’s what stands out to me most about libraries now, as an adult who has learned how unusual that really is. In most places, being allowed to take up space means you’re expected to buy something. Coffee shops want you to order a latte. Malls want you to leave with a receipt. Even parks come with rules and closing hours. The library alone says: come in, have a seat, stay as long as you want. It may be the last truly free room in American life, and I think we undervalue it because it asks so little in return.

People like to say libraries are obsolete now, that everything is online. But that misses the point of what a library actually is. Yes, it lends books, and that by itself is kind of miraculous: a shared shelf where one copy of a novel might make its way through fifty different hands. But spend just one afternoon in a library and you’ll see it doing so much more. A man in a worn jacket is filling out a job application on a public computer while a librarian patiently helps him attach his résumé. A teenager is doing homework there because she doesn’t have internet at home. A toddler is learning how to sit still for a story. One person is getting help with tax forms, another is learning English, and someone else is simply staying warm, out of the cold and safe for a few hours.

It’s an old idea, but it may be more necessary now than ever. We live in a time when information is everywhere and yet more and more of it is fenced off, hidden behind paywalls, filtered by algorithms that decide what we see. The library offers something very different. Its shelves are curated by people trained to help you find what’s true, not what will keep you scrolling. A librarian will answer your question without tracking you, selling your data, or nudging you toward an ad.

That winter, I made my way through the children’s section, then the adult section, then whatever a kind librarian pushed across the desk with a raised eyebrow and a simple, “Try this.” I read about places I would never visit and lives completely unlike my own. After a while, I stopped feeling like the new kid. I started feeling like I belonged to something bigger.

I still carry a library card, and it’s still one of my most prized possessions. To me, it’s proof of an agreement we made with each other: that we would pool our resources so everyone, no matter their circumstances, could have access to the world.

That agreement still exists. It’s worth holding on to.

In what many are calling a landmark act of repatriation, a major European museum has returned a collection of looted artifacts to their country of origin, a move seen as an important step in confronting the legacy of colonial-era plunder.

At a ceremony on Tuesday, the museum formally handed over 27 objects to Nigerian officials. The items included ceremonial sculptures, carved ivory pieces, and bronze plaques that were taken during a 19th-century military expedition. The artifacts had been kept in the museum’s African collections for more than a century and are expected to be displayed in Lagos once conservation work is finished.

Museum director Elise Hartmann said the return was both “a moral responsibility and an institutional reckoning.”

“These objects were acquired in circumstances that were deeply unjust,” Hartmann said. “They are not simply works of art; they are part of a living cultural heritage. Returning them is the right thing to do.”

The repatriation comes after years of pressure from Nigerian officials, scholars, and activists, who have long argued that artifacts seized during colonial campaigns should be restored to the communities they were taken from. Recent provenance research by the museum found that the objects were removed during a British punitive raid in 1897, then sold through European art markets before eventually entering the museum’s collection.

Nigeria’s Minister of Culture, Amina Bello, welcomed the return and called it “an important act of justice, dignity, and historical acknowledgment.”

“For generations, these treasures were admired abroad while the people to whom they belong were denied access to them,” Bello said. “Their return does not erase the past, but it helps us confront it honestly and begin to repair the damage.”

The decision is part of a broader shift among museums in Europe and North America, where many institutions are taking a closer look at the origins of items acquired during the colonial period. In recent years, several museums have announced the return of bronzes, sacred objects, and human remains after evidence showed they had been taken through violence, coercion, or theft.

Even so, the issue remains contentious. Some critics say museums serve a global public and should keep major collections while making them more widely available through loans and partnerships. Others argue that full repatriation is necessary to address long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Experts say this latest return could help spur similar actions elsewhere. “This is not just about one museum or one set of objects,” said art historian Daniel Okoye. “It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely.”

The museum said it will continue reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection and is already in discussions with other countries about possible returns.

For many observers, Tuesday’s handover was about more than the transfer of property. It was a public acknowledgment that the wounds of history can no longer be left behind glass.

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered mechanical device that is widely regarded as the earliest known analog computer. It was built to calculate and display astronomical phenomena, including the positions of the Sun and Moon, lunar phases, eclipse cycles, and possibly the movements of some planets. It is generally dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE.

The mechanism was discovered in 1901 in the remains of a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. It was recovered as a group of heavily corroded bronze fragments and at first drew only limited attention. Its extraordinary complexity did not become clear until decades later, when researchers found finely cut gears embedded in the fragments. Since then, modern imaging methods, especially X-ray computed tomography, have revealed much of its internal structure and inscriptions.

The device was enclosed in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its front face had circular dials with pointers that showed astronomical information, probably including the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar. It was likely operated by a hand crank that drove a system of more than 30 bronze gears. Those gears converted rotational motion into mathematical relationships that matched celestial cycles. The mechanism also modeled the Moon’s irregular motion with striking sophistication, using a pin-and-slot arrangement to simulate changes in lunar speed in a way that was consistent with ancient Greek astronomical theory.

On the back were spiral dials used to track longer-term cycles. One represented the Metonic cycle of 19 years, which reconciles lunar months with the solar year. Another tracked the Saros cycle, which was used to predict eclipses. A smaller subsidiary dial seems to have marked the Exeligmos, a longer eclipse cycle that improved prediction accuracy. Inscriptions on the device appear to have served as a kind of operating manual, explaining the purpose of the dials and astronomical displays.

The Antikythera mechanism shows a level of technical skill that was once thought impossible for the Hellenistic world. Its precise gearing points to a sophisticated tradition of instrument-making, even though no other surviving device from antiquity of comparable complexity is known. Scholars have connected it to Greek scientific traditions associated with figures such as Hipparchus, Posidonius, and Archimedes, although its exact origin and maker remain uncertain.

The mechanism has changed modern understanding of ancient science and technology. It demonstrates that Greek craftsmen and astronomers were capable of expressing advanced mathematical knowledge in an intricate mechanical form. Often described as “centuries ahead of its time,” the Antikythera mechanism remains one of the most celebrated archaeological discoveries in the history of science.

**The Street That Learned to Breathe**

The first time I was in a city center without cars, I didn’t notice what was missing right away. What I noticed were the sounds: a busker playing an out-of-tune accordion, a toddler squealing with delight at a pigeon, two older men bickering over a chess game. It took me about a minute to realize what I wasn’t hearing—the low, constant growl I’d always confused with silence.

This was in a mid-sized European city, on a trip I’d mostly taken to get away from my own. Back home, I drive everywhere. I’m not proud of that, but I’m not going to pretend I don’t. Downtown, for me, is something to get through: driving in circles looking for parking, paying too much once I find it, then walking half a mile past gray parking garages. So when people talk about banning cars from city centers, my gut reaction is to push back. What about groceries? What about my mother, who can’t walk very far? What about the plumber, the ambulance, the delivery driver?

Those are fair questions, and the best car-free city centers actually answer them. Ambulances and fire trucks can still get through. Residents with disabilities have permits and designated drop-off areas. Deliveries are handled in early-morning time slots. When it’s done well, a ban works less like a wall and more like a filter. It recognizes that the busiest and most valuable square mile in a city shouldn’t be built around the least efficient way of moving people through it.

Because it is inefficient. One lane of car traffic can move maybe 2,000 people an hour. Give that same amount of space to a tram or to pedestrians, and it can move many times more. We give up enormous amounts of prime real estate just to store empty cars, and then act surprised when rent is high and public space is hard to find.

Even so, I don’t think the answer is a simple yes. I’ve seen cities impose bans without offering anything in exchange: no dependable buses, no protected bike lanes, no affordable alternative at all. In those places, banning cars doesn’t create a vibrant public square. It punishes the night-shift worker commuting from the outskirts at midnight after the trains have stopped running. Cities that ban first and build later are mostly experimenting on their poorest residents.

So my position is conditional, but clear. Cities should move toward car-free centers, but they should earn that change by building the alternatives first, or at least at the same time. Make the train faster than driving. Make the bike lane feel safe enough for an eleven-year-old. Then close the street, and most people won’t have much reason to complain.

What changed my mind wasn’t data. It was standing in that European square at dusk, watching the chess players pack up and families move in, children darting between café tables without a parent gripping their shoulder. No one was rushing. No one was in danger. It hit me that I had never seen a city center feel like a living room before.

I still drive at home. But I’ve started parking on the edge of downtown and walking the rest of the way in. The first few times, it felt like giving something up. Now it feels like practicing for something better: a city where the center belongs to the people who are actually there.

Artemisia Gentileschi (8 July 1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter and is widely considered one of the most accomplished artists of her generation. Working in the tradition of Caravaggio, she became known for dramatic compositions, a naturalistic style, and powerful portrayals of heroic women drawn from myth, scripture, and history. She was also the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence.

Born in Rome, Artemisia was the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi and Prudentia Montone. Her mother died when Artemisia was about twelve years old. She trained in her father’s workshop, where she learned drawing, color mixing, and painting techniques. Since women were barred from formal academies, most of her education took place in the studio. Her earliest signed painting, *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), already showed remarkable skill for a seventeen-year-old.

In 1611, Artemisia was raped by Agostino Tassi, a painter and colleague of her father who had been hired to teach her perspective. Orazio brought charges the following year, and a seven-month trial began in 1612. During the proceedings, Artemisia was reportedly examined under torture with thumbscrews to verify her testimony. Tassi was convicted, but his sentence of exile from Rome was not enforced for long. The surviving trial transcripts remain a rare record of a woman’s testimony from that period.

Soon after the trial, Artemisia married the Florentine artist Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence. There she achieved considerable success, winning the patronage of Cosimo II de' Medici and becoming friends with Galileo Galilei. In 1616, she was admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Paintings from this period include *Judith Slaying Holofernes* (c. 1614–20) and *Self-Portrait as a Lute Player*.

Financial troubles and debt eventually brought her back to Rome in the 1620s, and she later worked in Venice and Naples. In 1638, she joined her father at the court of Charles I in England. After Orazio’s death in 1639, she completed some of his commissions. She spent much of her later career in Naples, where she collaborated with other painters and received prominent commissions.

Gentileschi’s work is distinguished by strong chiaroscuro, vivid color, and emotional intensity. She often painted women such as Judith, Susanna, Esther, Bathsheba, and Cleopatra. Her heroines are physically strong and psychologically complex, standing in contrast to the more passive portrayals often seen in the work of her male contemporaries.

After her death, Gentileschi was largely overlooked for centuries. In the 20th century, art historians—especially feminist scholars—rediscovered her work and reevaluated her importance. Since then, her life and art have inspired books, plays, and films, and major exhibitions, including one at the National Gallery in London in 2020, have firmly established her reputation as a leading master of the Baroque.

# Migration Guide: Config Format v1 → v2

Version 2 of the configuration format has a cleaner structure, stricter typing, and clearer naming. This guide walks through the main changes and explains how to update existing v1 files.

## Summary of Breaking Changes

1. Top-level keys are now organized into sections.
2. Several field names have changed.
3. Boolean and numeric values must use proper YAML/JSON types instead of strings.
4. Environment-specific overrides have moved into a dedicated `environments` block.
5. Deprecated v1 fields are no longer supported.

## Key Changes

### 1. Top-level structure

In v1, most settings were defined at the root level. In v2, they’re grouped into these sections:

- `server`
- `logging`
- `auth`
- `environments`

### 2. Renamed fields

Some of the most common renames are:

- `host` → `server.host`
- `port` → `server.port`
- `logLevel` → `logging.level`
- `logFile` → `logging.file`
- `enableAuth` → `auth.enabled`

### 3. Strict value types

In v1, string values like `"true"` or `"8080"` were often accepted. In v2, you need to use native types instead:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

In v1, environment-specific settings were often written as flattened keys like `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2, those settings belong under `environments`:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example Migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed Fields

These v1 fields are no longer supported in v2:

- `timeoutMs` — replaced by `server.timeout` in seconds
- `authModeLegacy` — removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug` — replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration Tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before deployment.
- Update any automation scripts that still read the old field names.
- Check for quoted booleans and numbers, since these now fail validation.
- If possible, migrate incrementally in a staging environment first.

## Final Checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the correct sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

Once you’ve made these updates, your configuration should be fully compatible with version 2.

    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example Migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

These v1 fields are no longer supported in v2:

- `timeoutMs` — replaced by `server.timeout` in seconds
- `authModeLegacy` — removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug` — replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration Tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before deployment.
- Update any automation scripts that still read the old field names.
- Check for quoted booleans and numbers, since these now fail validation.
- If possible, migrate incrementally in a staging environment first.

## Final Checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the correct sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

Once you’ve made these updates, your configuration should be fully compatible with version 2.

# photodate

`photodate` renames your photos based on the date they were taken. It reads EXIF metadata and renames files into a consistent, sortable format such as `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Uses the original capture date from EXIF data
- Falls back to the file’s modified time if EXIF data is missing
- Supports customizable filename templates
- Includes a dry-run mode so you can preview changes
- Automatically handles duplicate timestamps
- Lets you undo the most recent run
- Works with JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

Install with pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or install from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

`photodate` requires Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can point to one or more files or directories.

### Quick start

Preview the changes first:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Rename the files:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Process subfolders too:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Show the planned renames without changing anything |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | Process directories recursively |
| `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE` | Set the filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`) |
| `--fallback [mtime\|skip]` | Choose what happens when EXIF data is missing (default: `mtime`) |
| `--prefix TEXT` | Add a prefix to every filename |
| `--lowercase-ext` | Convert file extensions to lowercase |
| `--undo` | Revert the last run |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print every rename |

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%Y` | Four-digit year |
| `%m` | Month (`01–12`) |
| `%d` | Day of the month |
| `%H` `%M` `%S` | Hour, minute, second |

## Duplicate timestamps

Burst shots often end up with the same timestamp. If that causes a filename collision, `photodate` adds a counter:

```
2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_2.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_3.jpg
```

It never overwrites existing files.

## Undo

Each run writes a log to `~/.photodate/last_run.json`. To undo the most recent run:

```bash
photodate --undo
```

Only the most recent run can be undone.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before submitting changes.

## License

MIT

# Museum Returns 27 Looted Artifacts to Nigeria in Landmark Ceremony

**A group of Benin bronzes and ceremonial objects will be displayed in Benin City after spending more than a century overseas**

*Hartwell, England* — A regional museum in northern England officially returned 27 artifacts to Nigeria on Tuesday, bringing an end to a decade of negotiations over objects taken during a colonial-era military expedition in 1897.

In a ceremony attended by diplomats, museum staff, and members of the Edo diaspora community, the Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. The collection includes brass plaques, carved ivory pieces, and a ceremonial staff that once belonged to the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

“These are not simply objects,” said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, who led the Nigerian delegation. “They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes.”

The artifacts were originally taken in 1897, when British forces attacked Benin City and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many of those works were later sold at auction or dispersed among private collectors and institutions across Europe and North America. The Hartwell museum received its pieces in 1934 through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision came after extensive provenance research confirmed the objects’ origins beyond reasonable doubt. “We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us,” Marsh said. “The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible.”

The return comes as pressure continues to grow on Western institutions to confront colonial-era acquisitions. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States, and Scotland have returned parts of their Benin collections, while the British Museum still faces calls to return its much larger holdings.

The broader movement has not been universally embraced. Some curators argue that so-called universal museums give global audiences a chance to encounter a wide range of cultures in one place. Others have questioned whether receiving institutions have the capacity to conserve such works. Supporters of restitution, however, point to Nigeria’s development of the Edo Museum of West African Art, a major new facility designed by architect David Adjaye to house returned objects.

For Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent who attended the ceremony, the event carried deep personal meaning. “My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes,” he said. “I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime.”

The artifacts are scheduled to be flown to Lagos next week and then taken to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

Boredom gets a worse reputation than it deserves. We talk about it like it’s a small curse, something to avoid as urgently as hunger or loneliness. A boring class, a boring conversation, a boring afternoon—those things can feel like failures, as if life isn’t doing its job of keeping us entertained. For a long time, I saw it that way too. If I was waiting in line, riding the bus, or lying there staring at the ceiling with nothing pressing to do, I would reach for my phone almost without thinking. I treated every empty pocket of the day like a problem that needed fixing. It took me a while to realize that boredom isn’t always just emptiness. Sometimes it’s an opening.

When I was a kid, I ran into boredom in its purest form on summer afternoons. There were long stretches when it was too hot to play outside, there was nothing good on TV, and my friends were gone. At first, those afternoons felt unbearable. I can still remember wandering from room to room, telling anyone who would listen that there was “nothing to do.” But once I had complained myself out, something interesting usually happened. I’d start making strange little worlds out of whatever was around me: blankets turned into forts, notebooks became newspapers for imaginary cities, and a box of mismatched buttons became treasure. Boredom was the threshold I had to cross before my imagination could start working.

That didn’t go away when I got older; it just became harder to notice. Adult life gives us endless ways to escape boredom, and a lot of them are glowing right there in our hands. The second a task gets repetitive or a silence starts to linger, distraction is right there. But I’ve noticed that constant stimulation leaves me feeling oddly thin, like my attention has been split into so many fragments that none of it can fully land anywhere. Boredom does the opposite. It has a way of pulling me back together. It slows time down enough for thoughts I’ve been avoiding—or have just been too busy to hear—to finally surface.

Some of my clearest ideas have come to me in boring moments: folding laundry, walking the same familiar route, or sitting through the first uneventful minutes of a delayed train. In those moments, my mind begins to wander, and wandering isn’t the same as wasting time. A lot of the time, it’s where reflection begins. Boredom takes away the sense of urgency and makes room for a different kind of attention—less efficient, maybe, but wider and more open. It gives memory, curiosity, and even discomfort a chance to speak. Without it, I think I’d understand far less about what I actually think.

There’s a moral side to boredom too. Being bored means facing the fact that not every moment is meant to entertain us. The world doesn’t owe us constant novelty. Learning to tolerate tedium—to sit quietly in a waiting room, to stay present through a lull in conversation, to let an afternoon pass without demanding instant gratification—can be its own kind of patience. It teaches humility. It reminds us that a meaningful life isn’t made up only of exciting moments. It’s also made of ordinary stretches that ask for endurance, presence, and invention.

I still don’t always like being bored. I still reach for distraction more often than I want to. But I don’t see boredom as a void that needs to be filled as fast as possible anymore. I see it as a necessary pause, an interval where something quieter and more subtle can appear. In a culture that’s afraid of silence and obsessed with stimulation, boredom may be one of the last places where the mind can still hear itself think.

# Contributing Guide

Thanks for your interest in contributing to our open-source documentation website. We welcome all kinds of contributions, whether you’re fixing a typo, improving clarity, adding new content, or suggesting structural changes.

## Ways to Contribute

Here are some of the ways you can help:

- Fix spelling, grammar, or formatting issues
- Clarify existing explanations
- Add examples, tutorials, or reference material
- Report outdated or incorrect information
- Improve accessibility and readability
- Suggest better navigation or organization

If you’re not sure whether your idea is a good fit, feel free to open an issue first.

## Before You Start

Before jumping in, please take a moment to:

- Read through the existing documentation style and structure
- Search open issues and pull requests so you don’t duplicate work
- Check whether there’s already a discussion about the change you want to make

For larger changes, we recommend opening an issue before you start writing. It helps align expectations and can save time.

## Getting Started

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a new branch for your changes
3. Make your edits
4. Preview the site locally if possible
5. Commit your changes with a clear message
6. Open a pull request

Use descriptive branch names like `fix-installation-typo` or `add-api-auth-guide`.

## Writing Guidelines

To help keep the documentation consistent:

- Write in clear, direct language
- Use short paragraphs and descriptive headings
- Prefer examples over abstract explanations
- Keep terminology consistent across pages
- Link to related pages when it’s helpful
- Avoid unnecessary jargon

If you’re adding technical content, make sure your examples are accurate and easy to follow. If you include a command or code snippet, test it whenever possible.

## Style and Formatting

Please follow the project’s formatting conventions, including:

- Markdown structure and heading levels
- Code block formatting with language tags
- File naming patterns
- Internal linking style

If the repository includes linting or formatting tools, run them before submitting your pull request.

## Pull Request Expectations

A strong pull request should:

- Clearly explain what changed
- Explain why the change is needed
- Stay focused on a single topic when possible
- Include screenshots or previews for visual changes, if relevant

Be open to feedback. Reviews are a normal part of the process, and collaboration helps improve the final result.

## Reporting Issues

If you find a problem but don’t want to submit a fix, open an issue and include:

- A clear title
- A link to the affected page
- A description of the problem
- A suggestion, if you have one

## Code of Conduct

Please be respectful and constructive in all interactions. We want this project to feel welcoming to contributors of all experience levels.

## Thank You

Every contribution, big or small, helps make the documentation better for everyone. We appreciate your time, effort, and ideas.
