When people talk about the decline of letter writing, the first thing they usually bring up is nostalgia: the romance of envelopes, the elegance of stamps, the little thrill of recognizing someone’s handwriting before you’ve even read a word. All of that is real. But when we stop writing letters, we’re not just giving up a charming old ritual. We’re losing a way of thinking, a way of feeling, and a way of being present with one another.

Writing a letter asks something different of us than sending a text or an email. It asks us to be still long enough to figure out what we actually want to say. In most modern communication, speed is the whole point. We reply quickly, revise without anyone seeing, send half-formed thoughts, and rush to fill silence before it has a chance to deepen. A letter moves at the speed of reflection. Because it takes time to write, seal, send, and receive, it invites a kind of honesty that is less impulsive and more intentional. You usually don’t use a letter to talk about what you had for lunch or some passing annoyance. You collect yourself. You turn experience into language. And in the process, you often come to understand your own mind more clearly.

I think that’s one of the quietest losses: when we stop writing letters, we lose a private workshop for the self. A letter is not exactly a conversation, and it’s not exactly a diary. It lives in that intimate space between the two. It’s personal, but it’s also directed outward. You’re not revealing yourself into the void; you’re writing toward a particular person. That audience matters. In letters, we often become slightly better versions of ourselves—more thoughtful, more generous, more willing to explain what we mean. Writing to someone we love can refine not just our words, but our character.

Letters also hold feeling in a way instant messages rarely can. A text can say “I miss you,” but a letter carries physical proof that it was made by someone’s hands. The pressure of the pen, the slant of the lines, the crossed-out words, the note squeezed into the margin as an afterthought—those aren’t just decorative details. They’re traces of a living moment. A letter is language, but it’s also an object. It travels through weather and distance. It can be tucked into a drawer, reopened years later, and bring back a version of someone that seemed lost to us. To hold an old letter is to encounter not just what a person felt, but how they moved through time.

When we stop writing letters, we also lose some of our patience with absence. Letters teach us how to wait. And that waiting isn’t empty; it deepens affection. It gives longing space to ripen into attention. In an age when we can reach anyone instantly, we often come to expect access instead of presence. We mistake constant contact for closeness. But closeness doesn’t always grow out of frequency. Sometimes it grows out of concentration—from choosing words carefully, from speaking across silence instead of erasing it.

I don’t think we have to reject newer forms of communication in order to grieve what letters gave us. Texts are useful, emails are efficient, calls are immediate. But letters offered something these forms rarely do: a lasting record of thought shaped by time and care. When we stop writing letters, we lose not just an art, but a human rhythm. We lose one of the few forms of communication that asks us to slow down enough to truly mean what we say.

We lose one of the few forms of communication that asks us to slow down enough to truly mean what we say.

# Moving Configuration Files from v1 to v2

This guide walks through what changed between v1 and v2 of the configuration format and how to update your files. The examples below use YAML.

## What Changed

| Area | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Version field | Optional | **Required** (`version: 2`) |
| Server settings | Flat keys | Nested under `server` |
| Timeouts | Integers (seconds) | Duration strings (`"30s"`) |
| Environment variables | `$VAR` | `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` |
| Booleans | `yes`/`no` accepted | `true`/`false` only |
| `log_file` | Supported | Removed; use `logging.output` |

## Step 1: Add the Version Field

Start by adding this to the top of every file. In v2, parsers will reject any file that doesn’t include it.

```yaml
version: 2
```

## Step 2: Move Server Settings Under `server`

In v1, `host`, `port`, and `timeout` were top-level keys. In v2, they need to be grouped under `server`.

**v1**
```yaml
host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8080
timeout: 30
```

**v2**
```yaml
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  timeout: "30s"
```

## Step 3: Change Timeouts to Duration Strings

All time values now have to be written as strings that include a unit: `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`. Plain integers will now trigger a validation error, since the old default of treating them as seconds caused confusion.

## Step 4: Update Environment Variable Syntax

Replace `$DB_PASSWORD` with `${DB_PASSWORD}`. You can also provide fallback values now:

```yaml
database:
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
```

If you need a literal dollar sign, escape it as `$$`.

## Step 5: Replace Deprecated Options

`log_file` has been removed. Use the `logging` block instead:

**v1**
```yaml
log_file: /var/log/app.log
```

**v2**
```yaml
logging:
  output: /var/log/app.log
  level: info
```

## Step 6: Fix Boolean Values

Update `yes`, `no`, `on`, and `off` to `true` or `false`. v2 follows YAML 1.2, which no longer treats those older forms as booleans.

## Automated Migration

There’s a converter that can handle most of these updates for you:

```bash
config-tool migrate --from 1 --to 2 config.yaml -o config.v2.yaml
```

Before deploying, review the generated output. The tool can’t determine the correct `logging.level`, so it uses `info` by default.

## Validate the Result

```bash
config-tool validate config.v2.yaml
```

If there are any problems, fix the reported errors. The validator includes line numbers to help you find them.

## Rollback

Keep your v1 files around until v2 has been running successfully in production. v1 files will still work with v1-compatible releases, but v2 files are not backward compatible.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Unquoted durations:** `30s` works, but `30` fails.
- **Unescaped `$`:** Passwords that contain `$` may be interpreted as variables.
- **Mixed versions:** Any included files must all use the same version.

# Atacama Desert

The **Atacama Desert** (Spanish: *Desierto de Atacama*) is a desert plateau along the Pacific coast of western South America. It stretches for about 1,600 km (1,000 mi), mostly across northern Chile. It is widely considered the driest non-polar desert in the world and also one of the oldest continuously arid regions on Earth.

## Geography

The desert sits between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes Mountains, running from the southern border of Peru to roughly La Serena in Chile. It covers about 105,000 km² (41,000 sq mi), although some broader definitions that include nearby arid areas put its total size higher. Its landscape includes salt flats (*salares*), sand dunes, rocky plains, and volcanic peaks. In the eastern part of the region lies the Salar de Atacama, the largest salt flat in Chile.

## Climate

The Atacama’s extreme dryness comes from several factors working together. To the east, the Andes block moisture coming from the Amazon Basin. To the west, the cold Humboldt Current and a persistent subtropical high-pressure system limit rainfall from the Pacific. Some inland weather stations have never recorded rain, and many areas receive less than 15 mm (0.6 in) of precipitation a year on average. Evidence indicates that parts of the desert may have remained hyperarid for millions of years.

Even with these conditions, the coast often gets a steady fog called *camanchaca*, which supplies moisture to some plants and animals.

## Ecology

Plant life is limited, but the desert is home to highly specialized organisms, including cacti, lichens, and tough shrubs. In rare years with heavy rainfall, often associated with El Niño, parts of the desert burst into bloom in an event known as *desierto florido* (“flowering desert”). Animals found here include vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and many reptiles and insects. Scientists have also examined microbial life in the soils, which are sometimes compared to Martian soils.

## History and economy

Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures, lived in the region for thousands of years. In the 19th century, the desert became economically significant because of its nitrate (saltpeter) and guano deposits, both of which were important for fertilizer production. Competition for these resources helped drive the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), during which Chile gained territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Today, the economy is dominated by mining, especially copper and lithium. The Chuquicamata mine is one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

Because of its high elevation, dry atmosphere, and very low light pollution, the Atacama is one of the best places on Earth for astronomical observation. Major facilities there include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, which is home to the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Popular places to visit include San Pedro de Atacama, the Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and many high-altitude lagoons.

I never meant to become someone who walks everywhere. It started the week my car was in the shop and getting to the office by bus meant making a transfer that added forty minutes. So on one gray Tuesday, I left the house on foot, annoyed and grumbling, with only the vague plan of figuring it out as I went.

By about the third mile, I realized I hadn’t been alone with my own thoughts in years.

Walking creates a strange kind of attention. It’s too slow to be about arriving quickly and too active to feel like standing still. Your body has something to do, so your mind is free to wander. Problems I’d been tensing up over for weeks started to loosen on their own. I’d turn a corner and suddenly know how to phrase a difficult email, or understand that I’d been angry with my brother for the wrong reason. Nietzsche said that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. I don’t know about the great ones, but the useful ones do seem to show up that way.

When I got the car back, I kept walking anyway. Usually in the mornings, before the day started asking things of me. I got to know my neighborhood the way you get to know a person, not the way you memorize a map. There was the man who watered his tomatoes in a faded bathrobe and lifted one finger in greeting, like a conductor cueing a single violin. There was the corner where the smell of baking bread came through a vent at exactly 6:40. There was a persimmon tree I must have passed a hundred times before I noticed it was loaded with fruit, bright as lanterns against the bare branches. I kept wondering how much else I had driven past without ever really seeing.

The habit has its own quiet discipline. Some days it’s raining and I go anyway, and those often end up being the best walks: the streets washed clean and empty, my footsteps setting the rhythm. Some days I’m tired or sad and the walk doesn’t solve anything, but it does let me carry the sadness at a pace I can manage. I’ve learned that sorrow is easier to bear at three miles an hour.

I’ve also grown to love the math of it. A mile is about two thousand steps. A good walk is a few thousand more. None of those individual steps feels like much, and that’s the point. No one applauds a single step. But they add up, like pennies in a jar, into something real: a year of mornings, a body stronger than it used to be, a mind that feels a little less crowded.

I think a lot now about how much of modern life is built to save us effort and, in doing that, also save us from experience. Walking rejects that trade. It asks for your time and gives back something you didn’t realize you were missing: the feel of a place, the rhythm of your own breathing, the quiet peace of moving through the world at exactly your own speed.

Tomorrow morning, I’ll put my shoes on and go again. I have no idea what I’ll think about. That’s the whole point.

The Battle of Hastings took place on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army led by William, Duke of Normandy, and the English army of the Anglo-Saxon king Harold Godwinson. It was fought about 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, near what is now the town of Battle in East Sussex. The result was a decisive Norman victory, and it marked the start of the Norman Conquest of England.

The events leading up to the battle began in January 1066, when King Edward the Confessor died without children and set off a succession crisis. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost at once. William of Normandy, though, claimed that Edward had promised him the throne, and that Harold had sworn an oath to back his claim. At the same time, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada was also pressing a claim and invaded northern England in September 1066.

Harold marched north and defeated Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Just a few days later, on 28 September, William’s invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast. Harold then rushed his army south, covering about 250 miles in roughly two weeks.

At Hastings, Harold’s men took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill, where they formed a shield wall along the ridge. The English army was made up mostly of infantry, including the elite housecarls and the more lightly equipped fyrd. William’s army, by contrast, included infantry, archers, crossbowmen, and a large cavalry force.

The battle began in the morning. Norman archers shot uphill, but with limited success. Infantry and cavalry attacks followed, yet they were unable at first to break the English shield wall. At one stage, a rumour spread that William had been killed, and he is said to have lifted his helmet to prove he was still alive. Some Norman troops fell back, and some English soldiers chased them down the hill, only to be killed when the Normans turned back against them. Historians still debate whether these retreats were deliberate feigned retreats.

As the day went on, the English line began to weaken. Harold was killed late in the battle. Tradition says he was struck in the eye by an arrow, as shown in the Bayeux Tapestry, though that account is disputed. With their king dead, the English army broke and fled.

After the battle, William moved to secure his hold on the country. English leaders submitted to him, and he was crowned King of England on 25 December 1066 at Westminster Abbey. He later founded Battle Abbey on the battlefield itself. The Norman Conquest went on to bring major changes to English society, language, law, and landholding.

See also: Norman Conquest, Bayeux Tapestry, Battle of Stamford Bridge.

Commuters across the city ran into major delays and widespread disruption Tuesday after public-transit workers went on strike, bringing most bus, subway, and tram service to a halt.

The walkout began shortly after midnight, following weeks of failed contract talks between the Transit Workers Union and the Metropolitan Transit Authority. Union leaders said workers are pushing for higher pay, stronger job protections, and better staffing levels, saying employees have been under growing strain for years as living costs rise and labor shortages continue.

“This strike is a last resort,” union president Maria Delgado said at an early morning rally outside the transit authority’s headquarters. “Our members keep this city moving every day, but they are being asked to do more with less. We need a contract that reflects the value of their work and guarantees safe, reliable service for the public.”

Transit officials said they were disappointed by the strike and warned that if it lasts several days, it could have serious economic consequences. In a statement, the authority said it had offered a “fair and responsible” contract package that included wage increases and benefit protections, but said the union’s demands would put too much pressure on the transit system’s already stretched budget.

“We remain committed to reaching an agreement as quickly as possible,” said transit authority chief executive Daniel Mercer. “We urge union leadership to return to the bargaining table so we can restore service for the millions who depend on public transportation.”

By dawn, commuters were crowding rideshare pick-up areas, squeezing onto limited regional rail service, and lining up at bike-share stations. Streets downtown were heavily clogged as more residents turned to cars, taxis, and carpools to get to work. Several schools reported unusually high absentee rates, and some businesses said employees were arriving late or, when possible, working remotely.

City officials urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and announced temporary steps to reduce congestion, including expanded bike lanes, extra traffic officers at major intersections, and increased commuter-rail capacity. The mayor’s office also said it was watching the situation closely and encouraging both sides to return to negotiations with the help of a state-appointed mediator.

For many riders, the strike underscored just how central public transit is to daily life. “I understand why workers are upset, but this is chaos,” said commuter Jasmine Lee, who spent nearly two hours trying to get to her office. “So many people rely on these trains and buses. I just hope they settle this soon.”

Negotiations were expected to continue Tuesday afternoon, though neither side said how close they were to a deal. Until an agreement is reached, residents are preparing for more disruption and another uncertain commute.

Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter who is now considered one of the most important artists of the seventeenth century. She was one of the first women to achieve professional success in a field dominated by men, and she is especially known for her powerful portrayals of biblical and mythological heroines.

She was born in Rome and was the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, who gave her her earliest artistic training. Her work was deeply influenced by Caravaggio, particularly his dramatic use of light and shadow, emotional intensity, and naturalism. Even though women faced serious limits in artistic education at the time, Artemisia showed remarkable talent from a young age. One of her earliest known paintings, _Susanna and the Elders_ (1610), already reveals her striking ability to depict psychological tension and female experience.

A defining event in her life was the 1612 trial of Agostino Tassi, a painter who raped her. During the trial, Artemisia was subjected to public scrutiny and torture to confirm her testimony, and this episode has become central to many modern interpretations of her life and art. Not long afterward, she married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where her career took off. In 1616, she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno, an important mark of professional recognition.

During her time in Florence, and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples, Artemisia created many of her best-known works. Among them are _Judith Slaying Holofernes_, _Judith and Her Maidservant_, _Lucretia_, and _Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting_. Her paintings often focus on women from history, scripture, and legend at moments of crisis, courage, or revenge. While these themes were not unusual in Baroque art, Artemisia’s treatment of them has been widely admired for its intensity, dignity, and emotional complexity.

Artemisia also worked for elite patrons across Italy and beyond. She spent time in Naples, which became a major center of her later career, and she probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of Charles I of England. While there, she may have helped with court commissions before returning to Naples.

For many years after her death, Artemisia Gentileschi was overshadowed by her male contemporaries and was often remembered mainly in connection with her biography. Since the twentieth century, however, her reputation has grown enormously. Scholars have highlighted both her technical skill and her originality within Baroque painting. Today, she is celebrated not only as a pioneering woman artist, but also as a major painter whose work stands alongside that of the leading masters of her time.

During the trial, Artemisia was subjected to public scrutiny and torture to confirm her testimony, and this episode has become central to many modern interpretations of her life and art. Not long afterward, she married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where her career took off. In 1616, she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno, an important mark of professional recognition.

During her time in Florence, and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples, Artemisia created many of her best-known works. Among them are _Judith Slaying Holofernes_, _Judith and Her Maidservant_, _Lucretia_, and _Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting_. Her paintings often focus on women from history, scripture, and legend at moments of crisis, courage, or revenge. While these themes were not unusual in Baroque art, Artemisia’s treatment of them has been widely admired for its intensity, dignity, and emotional complexity.

Artemisia also worked for elite patrons across Italy and beyond. She spent time in Naples, which became a major center of her later career, and she probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of Charles I of England. While there, she may have helped with court commissions before returning to Naples.

For many years after her death, Artemisia Gentileschi was overshadowed by her male contemporaries and was often remembered mainly in connection with her biography. Since the twentieth century, however, her reputation has grown enormously. Scholars have highlighted both her technical skill and her originality within Baroque painting. Today, she is celebrated not only as a pioneering woman artist, but also as a major painter whose work stands alongside that of the leading masters of her time.

VoltHaus, an Austin-based home energy startup, said Tuesday that it is voluntarily recalling about 42,000 of its HearthCell 10 home battery units after finding a defect that can cause them to overheat and, in rare cases, catch fire.

The recall applies to units made between March 2022 and August 2023 and sold in the U.S. and Canada. VoltHaus said it has received 31 reports of overheating worldwide, including six cases where a unit smoldered or caught fire. No one has been injured, but two homeowners said there was minor damage to garage walls.

The company said the issue comes from a flaw in a batch of internal wiring connectors supplied by a third-party manufacturer. In certain situations, including repeated rapid charging in high temperatures, those connectors can wear down and create electrical resistance that produces too much heat.

“Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here,” VoltHaus co-founder and CEO Dana Okafor said in a statement. “We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost.”

The HearthCell 10, which sells for about $8,900 installed, stores solar power for use at night or during outages. VoltHaus says it has sold about 60,000 units since it launched in 2021, so the recall affects a substantial portion of the batteries it has installed.

Customers can find out whether their battery is included by entering the serial number on VoltHaus’s recall website. The serial number is printed on a label on the right side of the unit. For now, the company is telling owners of affected batteries to switch them to “limited mode” in the mobile app, which slows charging and helps reduce heat buildup until a technician can make the repair. Owners who can’t access the app are being urged to call the company’s dedicated hotline.

VoltHaus said technicians will replace the connectors, a repair that takes about two hours. The work is expected to start next week, with first priority going to homes where the batteries are installed in attached garages or living spaces.

Analysts say the recall could put pressure on the young company’s finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been getting ready for a public offering. “A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational,” said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. “How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself.”

A spokesperson said the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is reviewing the recall.

# csvkit-lite

csvkit-lite is a small, dependency-free Python library for parsing CSV files. It includes type inference, header handling, and streaming support.

## Requirements

- Python 3.8 or newer
- No third-party dependencies

## Installation

You can install it from PyPI with pip:

```bash
pip install csvkit-lite
```

If you want the latest development version, install it directly from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/example/csvkit-lite.git
```

If you prefer an isolated setup, use a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install csvkit-lite
```

To verify that the installation worked:

```bash
python -c "import csvkit_lite; print(csvkit_lite.__version__)"
```

## Quick Start

Say you have a file named `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,34,Boston
Bob,28,Denver
Carol,41,Austin
```

### Reading rows as dictionaries

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv

for row in read_csv("people.csv"):
    print(row["name"], row["age"])
```

By default, csvkit-lite treats the first line as a header and returns each row as a dictionary.

### Automatic type conversion

If you turn on type inference, numbers and booleans are converted automatically:

```python
rows = list(read_csv("people.csv", infer_types=True))
print(rows[0]["age"] + 1)   # 35, since age is an int
```

### Custom delimiters and headers

Use the `delimiter` option for tab-separated or semicolon-separated files. If the file does not include a header row, you can provide the column names yourself:

```python
rows = read_csv(
    "data.tsv",
    delimiter="\t",
    header=False,
    columns=["id", "score", "label"],
)
```

### Streaming large files

`read_csv` returns a generator, so rows are loaded lazily. That keeps memory usage low, even with large files:

```python
total = 0
for row in read_csv("huge.csv", infer_types=True):
    total += row["amount"]
print(total)
```

### Loading everything at once

If you would rather work with a plain list, just wrap the call:

```python
data = list(read_csv("people.csv"))
```

## Handling Errors

Malformed rows raise a `CSVParseError`, which includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

try:
    rows = list(read_csv("broken.csv"))
except CSVParseError as err:
    print(f"Problem on line {err.line}: {err}")
```

If you want to ignore bad rows, pass `skip_errors=True` instead.

## Next Steps

- Run the tests with `pytest`
- Read the full API reference in the `docs/` folder
- Report bugs on the GitHub issue tracker

Here’s what happened: on April 1, a lot of Netflix users reported seeing a weird “April Fool’s tax” added to their monthly subscription charges. Naturally, people were confused and frustrated by the unexpected fee. Some assumed it had to be a joke, while others were genuinely worried about being charged extra.

As it turned out, though, the “April Fool’s tax” was just a system glitch. Netflix responded quickly, confirmed that it wasn’t intentional, apologized for the confusion, and said the extra charge would be reversed on users’ next billing cycle.

It was definitely frustrating at first for the people affected, but in hindsight it’s also kind of funny that Netflix accidentally ended up pulling an April Fool’s prank this year. A lot of people went to social media to talk about their confusion, and later their relief once Netflix explained what had happened.

All in all, it was a harmless and pretty amusing situation. It’s a good reminder that even major companies like Netflix aren’t immune to unexpected glitches—or accidental pranks—on April 1. Did anyone else run into this “April Fool’s tax,” or something similar? Share your stories in the comments.

First, it helps to define what a “VA panel” actually is. VA, or Vertical Alignment, is a type of LCD panel that aligns the liquid crystals vertically to the subpixel layout rather than horizontally like traditional LCD panels. This alignment technology is known for high contrast ratios and deep blacks, which is why it’s popular with gamers and graphic designers.

There are a few reasons people might think VA panels are inferior:

1. Viewing angle: A common complaint is that VA panels have limited viewing angles, meaning the colors and contrast can shift if you’re not looking at the screen straight on. But this is often overstated. While it’s true that VA panels can have limited viewing angles, it’s really only an issue if the panel is poorly calibrated or if you’re sitting at an extreme angle. In practice, most people sit directly in front of their monitors, so for the vast majority of users, this isn’t really a problem.

2. Response time: Another criticism is that VA panels have slower response times than other panel types, like TN (Twisted Nematic) panels. That part is true, but response time isn’t the only thing that matters. If you’re a hardcore gamer who depends on lightning-fast reflexes, then slower response times could be a downside. Recentemente me mudei para a minha casa própria e tenho ido visitar minha mãe toda semana. Ela é uma senhora idosa que mora sozinha, mas de um tempo para cá comecei a perceber alguns sinais que estão me deixando preocupado.

Ela anda mais calada e sem o entusiasmo de antes. Às vezes aparece com hematomas que não sabe explicar, e fica nervosa quando tento perguntar sobre isso. Também percebi que o dinheiro da conta bancária dela está acabando bem mais rápido do que o normal, mesmo ela dizendo que não está gastando com nada diferente do habitual.

Não quero tirar conclusões precipitadas, mas estou sinceramente com medo de que alguém possa estar abusando dela, seja fisicamente ou financeiramente. Já tentei conversar com ela sobre isso, mas ela muda de assunto ou diz que é só descuido.

Sinceramente, não sei o que fazer. Alguém já passou por algo parecido ou tem algum conselho sobre como eu deveria agir? Me dói pensar que minha mãe possa estar em uma situação perigosa e que eu talvez não esteja fazendo nada para ajudá-la. Qualquer ajuda seria muito bem-vinda.

To the girl I may never get to love,

I hope you’re happy. I hope you’re doing well, surrounded by people who make you laugh and remind you how loved you are. I hope you’re spending your time doing what you love and chasing the dreams that matter to you.

Part of me wishes I could be the one to make you happy. I wish I could be the person you turned to when you needed a laugh, or when you needed someone to lean on. I wish I could be the one you shared your dreams with, the one beside you as you went after them.

But the truth is, I may never get to be any of those things. And that’s okay.

Because even if I’m never the one you love, it still means something to know that you’re happy. It means something to know you’re surrounded by people who make you laugh, who make you feel loved, and that you’re out there doing what you love and following your dreams.

And even if I never get to be the one you love, I still feel lucky. Lucky that our paths crossed at all. Lucky that I got to know the kind of amazing person you are. Lucky that, even if I may never get to love you, I can still be grateful knowing you’re out there, living your best life.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger has thrown his support behind troubled Romanian star Adrian Mutu, saying he still believes in his potential and urging clubs to give him a second chance.

Mutu, the former Chelsea striker, has had a turbulent career marked by drug scandals and suspensions. Even so, Wenger — long known for helping talented but troubled players — has made it clear he is willing to look past Mutu’s history.

“Every individual deserves a second chance,” Wenger said. “What does a child learn first at school? Forgiveness. That is vital in life as well. We all make mistakes, but we grow from them.”

Wenger also said there is no question about Mutu’s ability, and that his past should not define what comes next for him in football.

“He is a gifted player and his personal struggles should not overshadow his skill on the field,” Wenger said. “Football is about grit and resilience and Mutu has shown plenty of both through his battles.”

The former Arsenal boss, who developed many young players during his time in charge, believes Mutu could still become an exceptional player again if he gets the right support and guidance.

“Everyone deserves redemption and growth, yes, even in football,” he added. “Adrian's case is no different.”

Now 42, Mutu was once regarded as one of Europe’s top strikers. He was prolific for clubs such as Parma and Fiorentina, though he struggled at Chelsea. His career began to unravel after he failed a drug test in 2004 and was banned from professional football for seven months.

Although he was later reinstated, his reputation suffered another blow in 2010 when he tested positive again for a banned substance while playing for Fiorentina. He received a nine-month ban and never made it back to the top level of the game.

Wenger’s comments may come as a timely boost for Mutu, who has recently said he wants to stay involved in football as a coach. Whether Wenger’s backing will help spark a new chapter in the Romanian’s career remains to be seen.

Indian tennis has a new Wimbledon star. Vimal Mirza, the president of the Badminton Federation of India, made history as the first Indian woman to reach the singles semi-finals, but her run ended on Thursday with a quarter-final loss to Naomi Osaka. Mirza, who marked her 43rd birthday on the final day of the tournament, was beaten 6-1, 6-4 by the former world number one from Japan in what was her first Grand Slam semi-final.

“I just wanted to go out there and ball out and just go for it, see what happens,” said the higher-ranked Osaka, who reached the fourth round at SW19 last year. “For me, Grand Slams are usually hard, and I just wanted to try my best. I feel like everyone has been working very hard on their games, drilling day in, day out. To be able to have the opportunity to play a match like that, I’m very grateful. I’m not expecting to win, but I’m excited to play.”

The match was tight early on, and Mirza had several chances to break, but it was Osaka who found the key opening in the eighth game before serving out the set. The crowd got behind the home favorite, yet Osaka stayed composed, breaking twice early in the second set to close out the win.

“I just felt like I was struggling a little bit with my bounce, and she was so consistent with her bounce, like, hitting so many shots back,” said Osaka, who has now made the semi-finals in four of her last six Slams. “Yeah, I just felt like maybe I couldn’t get any spin. So I just tried to like focus on hitting it deeper, and that seemed to help.”

It also had a major impact on Ireland’s musical landscape and on contemporary harping.

Máire Ní Chathasaigh is a major figure in Irish music, especially in the world of the Irish harp. Known for her groundbreaking work on the instrument, she has been described by The Irish Times as “the doyenne of Irish harp players.” Ceol Aduaidh is a strong example of Ní Chathasaigh’s skill and individual style, and it helped open a new direction in Irish music.

Her ornate, rhythmic playing gives these regional tunes a rich and memorable character. In the end, Ceol Aduaidh is more than just an album; it is an important chapter in the history of Irish music. It was ahead of its time in reshaping the traditional sound and techniques of the Irish harp, and it confirmed Máire Ní Chathasaigh’s place as a key influence in the field. The album continues to inspire harpists and lovers of Irish music around the world.

Political jurisprudence is the study and philosophy of law and how it relates to politics and government. It is an interdisciplinary field that brings together law, political science, and philosophy to better understand the nature and operation of legal systems. It looks at questions like what law is, what purpose it serves, how it should be created and applied, and how it connects to political institutions and the broader social order.

1. Analytic jurisprudence: This approach centers on analyzing legal concepts and the logical structure of legal arguments. It aims to clarify the meaning and nature of legal terms and how they are used in legal reasoning.
2. Normative jurisprudence: This approach focuses on evaluating legal systems and their moral and political justification. It asks what the law ought to be, how it should be made, and how it should be applied.
3. Critical jurisprudence: This approach challenges the idea that law is neutral and objective. It argues that law is shaped by social and political power relations and that legal systems often help preserve the interests of dominant groups in society.

She was born on September 12, 1942, in California, USA, and was raised in a family of Chinese immigrants. Although she faced discrimination early in life, she remained determined to follow her interest in science and later earned her Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania.

After finishing her doctorate, Yuen Maul built a career in academia, serving in a range of roles at institutions including the University of California, San Francisco, and the Yale University School of Medicine. Her research has centered on genetic disorders, especially inherited defects of the liver. More recently, she has been credited with discovering an inherited genetic disorder involving mitochondrial DNA.

Beyond her research, Yuen Maul has been a strong voice for diversity in science and an important role model for women in the field. Her contributions have been recognized with many awards and honors, including the Distinguished Scientist Award from the American Association of Liver Diseases and the NIH Research to Prevent Alcoholism Award.

Amelia Jones is widely recognized as a groundbreaking scholar whose work has made a major impact on Art History, Art Theory, and Visual Culture. Over the course of several decades, she has built an extensive body of scholarship and helped reshape academic conversations around feminist art history and queer theory.

Born in 1965 in Springfield, Illinois, Jones was fascinated by art from an early age. She studied art history at Yale University and earned her undergraduate degree there in 1987. Continuing to follow her passion for art, she went on to complete a Ph.D. in Visual and Cultural Studies at the University of Rochester in New York in 1992.

Jones began her academic career as a professor of Visual Culture at the University of Manchester, where she taught from 1998 to 2007. She later moved to the University of Southern California, where she currently serves as the Robert A. Day Professor of Art & Design and Vice Dean of Critical Studies.

Her scholarship is known for its interdisciplinary approach and engages a wide range of subjects, including feminist art, body art, performance art, and film. Drawing on both contemporary and historical perspectives, Jones often challenges conventional assumptions and offers new ways of interpreting art.

She has written and edited several influential books, including "Body Art: Performing the Subject," which is credited with reshaping discussions of performative art, and "Seeing Differently: A History and Theory of Identification in the Visual Arts." She also edited the important volume "The Feminism and Visual Culture Reader."

Beyond her books, Jones’s ideas and analysis have appeared in numerous scholarly journals. She has also lectured internationally at prominent institutions such as the Tate Modern and the Museum of Modern Art, reaching a wide audience of scholars, artists, and art enthusiasts.

A defining feature of Jones’s work is her commitment to feminist and queer theory, which she uses as a lens for engaging with and critiquing both historical and contemporary art. She argues for the importance of “seeing differently,” maintaining that art must be understood in relation to the viewer’s identity and that aesthetics cannot be separated from social and political contexts.

Through her incisive critiques and reinterpretations of visual culture, Jones has established herself as a trailblazer in art history. She has helped bring greater attention to underrepresented artists and art forms while advancing feminist and queer discourse in the arts. Through her extensive scholarship, she has influenced not only academic theory but also museum curatorial practices around the world.

He started his football career at Del Campo High School, where he quickly made a name for himself as an exceptional player. Hicks was a three-year starter and earned the league’s Defensive MVP award during his senior year. After a strong high school career, he received a scholarship to play college football at Louisiana State University.

At LSU, Hicks kept building his reputation as a dominant defensive lineman. Over two seasons, he played in 26 games and totaled 69 tackles, six sacks, and three forced fumbles. His play drew the attention of NFL scouts, and he chose to give up his remaining eligibility to enter the 2012 NFL Draft.

Away from football, Hicks has also made a positive impact through his charitable work. He founded the Akiem Hicks Foundation, which is dedicated to empowering and inspiring underserved youth through education and athletics. Through the foundation, he has organized a range of initiatives, including scholarship programs and community service events.

Akiem Hicks’ career and contributions to football have earned him recognition and respect from both his peers and fans. With his talent and dedication to the game, he continues to be a force on the football field.

“Judicial murder” is the term used when court proceedings are misused to bring about the unjust execution of a person, often for political reasons. Even though it may appear to follow legal procedure, it departs sharply from any real standard of justice, usually because the judicial system is corrupt or biased.

At the heart of the idea is the concept of a wrongful execution, which violates the most basic human right: the right to life. Several related labels fall under this umbrella, including “miscarriage of justice,” “legal homicide,” and “state-sanctioned murder.”

In essence, judicial murder is a paradox. The judiciary is supposed to protect the lives and rights of citizens. But in cases of judicial murder, the court instead becomes complicit in an unlawful killing, betraying its most fundamental duty.

Judicial murder is not a modern phenomenon. Such cases go back to classical history and appear across different eras, cultures, and countries. Frequently cited examples include the execution of Jesus Christ, which some legal historians regard as a case of judicial murder, the execution of Marie-Antoinette during the French Revolution, and the execution of Socrates in ancient Greece.

In more recent history, a number of these cases have become especially well known because of the political motives behind them and the broader implications of the executions. The execution of political dissidents under authoritarian regimes, for example, often involves manipulated court proceedings that fit the definition of judicial murder.

Today, these cases often draw international condemnation and intense media coverage because of how controversial they are. The attention is often heightened when high-profile political figures are involved.

Judicial murder highlights a profound clash between law and justice. In these cases, an execution may be legal under the laws of the state, yet still be unjust by the standards of human rights. That tension feeds into the broader debate over capital punishment, wrongful convictions, and the extent to which judicial systems are vulnerable to bias.

Preventing judicial murder requires independent and transparent courts, fair trials, and stronger evidentiary standards. Abolishing the death penalty would also largely remove the possibility of judicial murder, and many countries around the world have already taken that step.

Even so, judicial murder continues to occur in the present day, underscoring persistent problems in justice systems around the world. That is why confronting the forces that lead to it remains essential.
